articles.title: Philippines requests 6 Chinook helicopters under $2-B US financing
articles.summary: The Philippine government, through the Department of National Defense (DND), has requested the purchase of six CH-47 Chinook helicopters under the $2-billion US Foreign Military Financing, Defense…

blocks.text: Published November 26, 2026 5:54pm

The Philippines, through the Department of National Defense (DND), has requested the purchase of six CH-47 Chinook helicopters under the $2-billion US Foreign Military Financing, Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro said on Thursday.

“Nag-request kami sa US government doon sa $2-billion financing ng anim na Chinook. That is the only thing I can disclose out of that package,” Teodoro said after the closing ceremony of the Armed Forces of the Philippines’ Joint Exercise Dagat-Langit-Lupa.
(We made a request to the US government regarding the $2-billion financing for six Chinooks. That is the only thing I can disclose out of that package.)
He said that all six brand-new helicopters could be delivered as early as 2029 if the US agrees to prioritize the Philippine order; otherwise, delivery could take up to six years.
Aside from the acquisition, the request also covers integrated logistics support and crew training.
Teodoro said a Chinook helicopter could carry about four times the load of a Black Hawk, pointing out the time and logistical space it would save.

“A Chinook can carry about 4 times a Black Hawk, so it saves you time, and it saves you logistical space. Kasi hindi minamano-mano ‘yan. Nilo-load na lang ng ano yan, ng lifter, loader,” the Defense chief said.
(A Chinook can carry about four times a Black Hawk, so it saves you time, and it saves you logistical space. Because you don't load that manually—it's loaded using a lifter or loader.)

“So, time is more than a quarter of one-fourth the time na kailangan mong i-load yung Black Hawk. 'Yun lang ang kailangan mo sa Chinook. Kaya mong magbuhat ng malalaking kanyon. Kaya mo magbuhat ng sasakyan na may pasahero pa,” he added.

(So, loading takes less than a quarter of the time you need to load a Black Hawk. That’s all you need for a Chinook. You can carry large artillery pieces, and you can even carry a vehicle with passengers still inside.)
However, Teodoro raised concerns about the helicopters’ maintenance costs, which he sees as a bigger challenge than building basing infrastructure for the aircraft.
“Basing ng anim na Chinook, e kayang-kaya. Maintenance, maintenance problema dun,” he said.
(Basing six Chinooks—we can easily manage that. Maintdenance is the problem there.)

Last week, the White House announced that Manila and Washington had agreed to work toward a foreign military financing loan exceeding $2 billion to supply the Philippines with defense and security capabilities from US suppliers. –Lyjah Tiffany Bonzo/NB, GMA News

blocks.text: World·New

There were no reports of injuries after the plane ran off the runway at about 8:40 p.m. ET, the airport reported. By early Thursday, the Federal Aviation Administration was reporting hourslong flight delays.
Incident occurs nearly 3 months after Amazon cargo jet overshot runway in Miami, killing 5 on ground
A FedEx airplane overran a runway at the Miami International Airport on Wednesday night, forcing all but one runway to temporarily close the day before American Thanksgiving, according to officials.

There were no reports of injuries after the plane ran off the runway at about 8:40 p.m. ET, the airport reported. The incident happened almost three months after an Amazon cargo jet overshot another runway in Miami, killing five people on the ground.
By early Thursday, the Federal Aviation Administration was reporting hourslong flight delays.
The FAA, which is investigating, said the McDonnell Douglas MD-11 was coming from Memphis.

items: Amazon suspends use of cargo carrier whose plane careened off Miami runway

blocks.text: FedEx said the plane had "an issue upon landing" and that it is coordinating with investigating officials.
"We are grateful that our crew is safe and there are no reported injuries," the company said in a statement.

FedEx had just started flying MD-11s again in May to deliver packages after that type of plane crashed in Kentucky last year as it was taking off. The UPS plane's left engine flew off and three pilots along with 12 people on the ground were killed. The FAA had approved Boeing's proposed fix for the MD-11s "after extensive review."

Responders investigate the cockpit of the cargo plane after it overran a runway at the Miami airport. By early Thursday, the Federal Aviation Administration was reporting hourslong flight delays. (Rebecca Blackwell/The Associated Press)
The airport recommended that passengers scheduled to fly Wednesday night should check with their airlines for the latest flight updates before travelling to the airport.
"We appreciate our passengers' patience as we work to safely resume normal operations," the airport said in a statement.

But three of Miami's runways converge at the west end, so the FedEx plane ended up close to where the Amazon plane careened across a road and struck a van filled with a plane-cleaning crew.

The incident also comes less than two weeks after a minor collision between two planes at a taxiway intersection at the Miami airport. The wing of the Copa flight and the nose of the UPS plane collided.
Miami-Dade Fire Rescue units responded to the incident Wednesday. The National Transportation Safety Board said it had no information about the situation.

blocks.text: This is a roundup of the top news stories from Germany on Thursday, November 26, 2026:
November 26, 2026
Parliament continues budget debates
The Bundestag is conducting its concluding debates on the budget for 2027 ahead of a final vote scheduled for Friday.

On Thursday, the focus will initially be on the individual budget for the Interior Ministry led by Alexander Dobrindt of the conservative Bavarian Christian Social Union (CSU), the sister party of Chancellor Friedrich Merz's Christian Democrats (CDU).

The government foresees that the ministry, which is responsible for the federal police and the domestic intelligence agency BfV, among other things, will receive some €16.8 billion in 2027 ($18.43 billion), around €1 billion more than this year.

Lawmakers will then go on to debate the individual budgets for the Economics and Energy Ministry, the Ministry for Housing, Urban Development and Building, the Ministry of Food and Agriculture and the Ministry for Education, Family Affairs, Senior Citizens, Women and Youth.

Opening the debates on Wednesday, Merz described the tight budget as an "accurate reflection" of the "difficult situation as a country — geopolitically, technologically, and demographically" — that Germany finds itself in.
"We will no longer be able to afford everything with tax revenue that we have become all too accustomed to for far too long," Merz added.

articles.title: How the Nvidia scandal is testing Singapore’s role in global chip trade
articles.summary: The Nvidia crisis has put Singapore squarely in Washington’s sights amid concerns over its role in China’s access to advanced AI chips. Here’s what’s at stake for the Southeast Asian nation and why…

image.caption: Singapore has come under scrutiny in the wake of the Nvidia scandal for not being vigilant enough in stopping the routing of advanced AI ships subject to U.S. export bans through its territory. Singapore-based Megaspeed, whose office is seen above, is one of the companies accused of facilitating the

blocks.text: World·New

The Nvidia crisis has put Singapore squarely in Washington’s sights amid concerns over its role in China’s access to advanced AI chips. Here’s what’s at stake for the Southeast Asian nation and why it’s stepping up efforts to prevent companies like Megaspeed, which was tied to one of the figures at the heart of the scandal, from circumventing U.S. export controls.
Singapore-based Megaspeed's role in Nvidia crisis has put scrutiny on diversion of chips to China

The Nvidia crisis has put Singapore squarely in Washington's sights amid concerns over its role in China's access to advanced AI chips. Here's what's at stake for the Southeast Asian nation and why it's stepping up efforts to prevent companies from circumventing U.S. export controls by diverting chips through its jurisdiction.

Prior to the emergence of the news that the CEO of chip giant Nvidia had an affair with a former executive of Singapore-based cloud computing company Megaspeed who may have been spying for China, Singapore had positioned itself as a key intermediary in the global AI supply chain.
The city-state benefited from its access to advanced U.S. chips and its established commercial ties with Chinese technology companies.

Singapore accounted for 22 per cent of Nvidia's global revenue last year, according to its financial filings before it stopped disclosing its Singapore sales and revenue. That's despite the fact that the vast majority of the products billed here were shipped elsewhere.
But allegations that Megaspeed diverted advanced AI chips to China have raised a critical question: were businesses here doing enough to verify where the hardware was ultimately going?

Alice Huang, seen in screenshot from a video provided by Taiwanese broadcaster TVBS, is suspected of spying for China while having an affair with Jensen Huang, CEO of Nvidia. Here, they are seen at a restaurant in Taipei, Taiwan, in May 2025. (TVBS/The Associated Press)

"That question was never asked: When you do business, would you ask where the thing goes? said Mark Goh, a professor of analytics and operations at the National University of Singapore's business school.
"When the money comes in and nothing is rocking the boat, you say, 'Fine, we'll do it,'"

items: Why Trump's move to get Jensen Huang reinstated won't end the questions
What the Nvidia scandal means for your investments

blocks.text: Now, Singapore is having to rethink its approach. It has launched an investigation into Megaspeed and said it's co-operating with U.S. authorities, who have been looking into the company's alleged diversion of chips to China since 2024 and added it to its trade blacklist earlier this week.
Why Nvidia couldn't afford to lose Jensen Huang | About That
Singapore's access to U.S. tech at risk
What's at stake isn't just its reputation as a trusted global trading hub but its continued access to advanced U.S. technology and its ambitions to become a leading AI hub.

Earlier this week, Prime Minister Lawrence Wong said Singapore was working closely with Washington to improve information sharing and set up a mechanism allowing U.S. authorities to conduct checks and enforce its own export controls.

Singapore's prime minister, Lawrence Wong, seen in Jakarta, Indonesia, in July 2026, said he is co-operating with U.S. authorities in efforts to clamp down on the diversion of AI chips to China through the Southeast Asian country. (Yasuyoshi Chiba/AFP/Getty Images)
But tighter enforcement will require greater visibility over a complex global supply chain.

One of the biggest challenges is tracking what happens to the chips after the initial sale. While suppliers are required to carry out checks on their customers, those customers may subsequently resell the chips to restricted parties.

"From a legal point of view, the selling company is not liable for the onward resale as long as the proper due diligence was carried out," said Goh Puay Guan, an associate professor specialising in supply chain management at NUS business school.
'They can't open every container'
Preventing the diversion of sensitive technology will likely require more stringent checks on end users.
For businesses in Singapore, that could mean higher compliance costs, longer transaction times and greater risks associated with doing business with Chinese technology companies.
The biggest concern for Singapore, perhaps, is losing its appeal as an intermediary between the world's two largest economies.
Shipping containers are seen at the port in Singapore. Local authorities are under pressure to step up monitoring of AI chips being shipped through the city-state. (Adrian Wyld/The Canadian Press)
"They need to keep the trust with both parties," said Matthias Hendrichs, an independent AI industry adviser.

"They need to step up the investigations and the monitoring they do.... At the same time, there can't be 100 per cent follow-up. They can't open every container that comes into the Singapore harbour."
U.S. moves to restrict cloud computing access
But it's not just the physical movement of chips that Singapore is now under pressure to monitor.

Washington is also moving to close a loophole in its export controls. Until now, Chinese technology companies could access advanced U.S. chips legally by renting computing power from overseas data centres.
That demand has helped fuel Southeast Asia's data-centre boom, with investment in Singapore alone forecast to reach $7 billion US this year, according to research by PwC and Oxford Economics.

items: How China gets around the U.S. ban on Nvidia chips

blocks.text: Under the new U.S. restrictions, data-centre operators serving major Chinese AI customers have until mid-February to secure licences or risk losing access to advanced chips.

Separately, the Financial Times, citing people familiar with the matter, reported that Nvidia had instructed its manufacturing partners to halt shipments of servers to Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand and Indonesia.

Malaysian customs officers stand next to a seized server containing advanced AI chips last month. The Financial Times reported Wednesday that Nvidia is halting shipments of servers to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia. (Vincent Thian/The Associated Press)
It is unclear how long the suspension will last, but it adds to the uncertainty facing the region's data-centre industry and risks delaying new projects.

"If projects lose anchor customers or cannot assure lenders that they have a reliable chip supply, financing could be delayed or fall through," said Han-Wei Liu, an associate professor of law at Singapore Management University.

items: Trump administration blacklists Megaspeed
U.S. further restricts China's access to AI chips in wake of Nvidia scandal

blocks.text: "That could slow the expansion of computing capacity across Southeast Asia and make it harder for local firms and researchers to develop AI."
Higher compliance costs could also eat into the profits of existing operators.
For Singapore, it adds to growing uncertainty over its future in the global AI supply chain.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Patrick Fok is director of APAC Strategy and Beijing correspondent for Feature Story News, a global broadcasting agency headquartered in Washington, D.C. A native of Hong Kong, he previously worked for Reuters and Channel NewsAsia in Singapore.

articles.title: Russia-Ukraine war extends to the Baltic and the Mediterranean
articles.summary: By attacking Russian vessels around the world, Kyiv is trying to up the pressure on Moscow and also sending out signals to its Western allies. What is the impact on global maritime trade?

image.caption: The Russian corvette Merkury was attacked by a Ukrainian drone called Sea BabyImage: Security Service of Ukraine/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: First there was an attack on a Russian cargo vessel, the Sparta II, off the Finnish coast, then on the Russian corvette Merkury and a dry cargo vessel that was allegedly carrying weapons off the coast of Libya. These spectacular Ukrainian operations in regions far from the Ukrainian capital Kyiv have caused a stir. They came shortly after several suspected Russian missiles crashed in Poland, not far from where an international military exercise was underway.
Intelligence agencies have long warned that Russia was preparing some form of provocation along NATO's eastern flank.
What are the risks of Russia's war in Ukraine escalating further and drawing in other regions?

It is no secret that Russia has long since expanded its operations beyond Ukraine: With military provocation, hybrid operations and acts of sabotage, Moscow has attempted to put pressure on the countries that openly support Ukraine.
And Ukraine has also targeted Russia's military and economy beyond its borders.

Since the summer, attacks by both Russia and Ukraine have increased in the Black Sea. Not only have Russian and Ukrainian cargo ships been targeted, but also vessels from other countries, particularly Turkey.

Furthermore, in the past few years, Ukraine has managed to deal significant blows to Russia, deep within Russian territory, thanks to aerial and maritime drones. It has targeted military airfields and other strategic targets such as oil refineries, including one in Omsk, Siberia, as well as military vessels in the eastern Black Sea.

blocks.caption: The Russian cargo vessel Sparta II was attacked off the Finnish coast Image: Finnish Border Guard/Handout/Lehtikuva/SIPA/picture alliance

blocks.text: Ukrainian attacks in Baltic Sea region

Russia has access only to a very narrow strip of the Baltic Sea coast, which is flanked by Finland and Estonia. Even ahead of the attack on the Sparta II, Ukraine had struck in the area multiple times, targeting oil terminals in the region around St. Petersburg, in Ust-Luga and Primorsk.
Russia uses the Baltic Sea to transport supplies to its Kaliningrad exclave and to export oil and other goods to the rest of the world, with the help of its "shadow fleet."

Ukrainian special forces are also said to have carried out operations against Russian military facilities in Syria, well before the fall of the Assad regime in December 2024. They are also reported to have lent support to local Tuareg fighters in Mali who were able to inflict heavy losses on the Malian army and allied Russian mercenaries.
Kyiv is thus attempting to harm Russia's military and economy worldwide, even if in military terms this does not help Ukraine directly.

The Russian corvette that was sunk was part of Russia's Black Sea Fleet but because of Turkey's blockade of the Bosporus and the Dardanelles, it would not have been allowed to return to the Black Sea. Instead, it was escorting Russian cargo ships in the Mediterranean. Primarily, the attacks send a political message: Russian ships can no longer feel safe — anywhere in the world.
Black Sea drone strikes put key global trade route at risk
Could war become omnipresent?

"We are not speaking about random shadow vessels which simply transport oil above the price cap and as a result bring revenues for the Russian treasury," security expert Elisabeth Braw from the Atlantic Council told DW. Sparta II was suspected of carrying military equipment, which Moscow denies.

"Ukraine is showing that it knows exactly, and secondly that it's able to hit them wherever and whatever waters they are in," Braw continued. "And this is something I don't think Ukraine has been able to do at the beginning of the war."

Officially, Kyiv's goal is to disrupt Russian logistics and supply routes, but military experts and politicians also see the attacks as a clear political signal to Western allies. They suspect that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy is sending a clear message of strength with an eye toward possible future peace negotiations.

In an interview on the German news outlet Tagesschau, security expert Joachim Weber from the University of Bonn suggested that Zelenskyy was paying less attention to the US, out of a sense of disappointment. He said that Ukrainian attacks in distant maritime areas were a sign that there was less inhibition and that Ukraine was ready to expand the conflict geographically to increase pressure on Russia, despite the risks.

Weber warned that war could become omnipresent if there was an increase in attacks on civilian vessels or ships that were considered suspicious in international waters. He said that Russia was providing more military escorts for the ships of its shadow fleet. "The likelihood that an accidental exchange of fire between armed forces, coast guards or anyone could occur is rising."

Braw pointed out that violations of the Law of the Sea were not only rising with regard to the Russia-Ukraine war but also in relation to other conflicts and playing out in "the South China Sea, the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea."

She said about 90% of global trade today was conducted via the oceans and she feared that others might conclude it was not "really to their advantage" to follow the rules of international maritime law.
She added that they might find it "beneficial in the short term to violate maritime rules" for short-term gains. "That would make the world's oceans significantly less safe for everybody."
This article was translated from German.
How Ukraine fights in the Black Sea without a navy

articles.title: Why did Mandaluyong buy 27 cars worth over P1 million each for barangays?
articles.summary: After the backlash, one of the barangays used the car for distributing free lettuce

blocks.text: HYBRID CARS. Vehicles for Mandaluyong barangays.
After the backlash, one of the barangays used the car for distributing free lettuce
Mandaluyong City has a new set of wheels for its barangay officials. These are not the usual vehicles you will see in a barangay hall’s garage.
On Monday, November 23, the city distributed 27 hybrid cars to its 27 barangays.
Mayor Menchie Abalos said that “these cars are long overdue for the barangay captains.”

“Gagamitin nila ‘yung sasakyan na ‘yan pang-service rin. Alam mo naman kapag barangay captain, saan-saan sila nauutusan. Saan-saan din sila nakakapunta. So this one, kinakailangan nila,” Abalos said in an interview during the distribution.

(They will also use that vehicle as a service vehicle. You know how it is when you’re a barangay captain —they get sent on errands all over the place, and they also have to go to various locations. So this one, they really need it.)
Based on photos from the event, the vehicles appear to be Jaecoo J5. According to AutoDeal, the model is priced at around P1.099 million.
The J5 comes with a 13.2-inch touchscreen infotainment system. Oh, and it has a sunroof, too.
The city government said the vehicles would help barangays respond more quickly to residents’ needs and deliver public services more efficiently.
Their primary uses include barangay patrols to maintain peace and order, responding to emergencies, and transporting essential services to residents.
But the purchase did not sit well with people online who raised questions about the need for vehicles costing more than P1 million each.

In response to the criticism, the Mandaluyong City government said in a statement on Wednesday, November 25, that the multipurpose vehicles were intended to serve the entire barangay, not just its captain.

“Pangunahing gamit nito ay ang pagroronda para mapanatili ang kapayapaan at kaayusan, agarang pagtugon sa pangangailangan ng residente o emergencies at paghahatid ng mga pangunahing serbisyo sa mamamayan,” the city government said.
(Its primary uses are patrolling to maintain peace and order, responding immediately to residents’ needs or emergencies, and delivering basic services to citizens.)
The city government maintained that the acquisition followed government procurement processes and regulations.
It said the decision considered the vehicles’ potential to reduce fuel consumption in the long run and lessen their environmental impact.
The city assured residents that it would monitor the use of the vehicles and not allow them to be used for personal purposes.
Barangay Daang Bakal, meanwhile, appeared to have a response to the criticism.
After the backlash, the barangay posted a video showing its new vehicle being used to distribute free lettuce to residents.
“Gamit ang ating bagong Barangay Service Patrol na J5 na pinag-usapan ng madlang people. Basta tama ang gamit, masustansyang buhay ang makakamit!” the barangay wrote in a Facebook post.
(Using our new J5 Barangay Service Patrol that everyone has been talking about. As long as it’s used properly, a healthy life will be achieved!)
Well, at least the new car is already making rounds.
But did barangay operations really require 27 vehicles worth over P1 million each? – Rappler.com

articles.title: Over 1,800 inmate records await review for parole, clemency
articles.summary: In a statement on Thursday, November 26, Catapang disclosed that a total of 1,893 carpetas—or inmate case records—remain pending before the board.

blocks.text: November 26, 2026 | 5:10pm
The front gate of the New Bilibid Prison in Muntinlupa City.
muntinlupacity.gov.ph

MANILA, Philippines — Nearly 1,900 case records of persons deprived of liberty (PDLs) submitted by the Bureau of Corrections are currently awaiting review by the Board of Pardons and Parole (BPP), BuCor Director General Gregorio Pio Catapang Jr. said.
In a statement on Thursday, November 26, Catapang disclosed that a total of 1,893 carpetas, or inmate case records, remain pending before the board.
Of this number, 1,513 are up for parole consideration, while 380 are being evaluated for executive clemency.
Catapang issued the clarification to dispel misconceptions that the BPP is waiting for BuCor to transmit prison records, noting that the board has the capacity to review up to 500 carpetas per month.

To streamline the evaluation process prior to submission, Catapang said BuCor has established a Management, Screening, and Evaluation Committee across all prisons and penal farms nationwide, each headed by its respective prison superintendent.

To streamline the evaluation process prior to submission, Catapang said BuCor has established a MSEC across all prisons and penal farms nationwide, each headed by its respective prison superintendent.

At the New Bilibid Prison, which holds the largest inmate population among the country's penal colonies, separate MSECs operate within its Minimum, Medium, and Maximum Security Camps, led by their respective camp commanders.

These committees are tasked with screening, evaluating, and recommending PDLs for time allowances, early release, parole, or executive clemency based on their behavior, rehabilitation progress, length of imprisonment, and compliance with existing rules.
From July 2022 to Oct. 15, 2026, 6,491 PDLs have been granted parole, according to the Department of Justice.
In the same period, 2,275 have been recommended for executive clemency, while 150 PDLs have been granted executive clemency.
As of August 2026, the congestion rate in Philippine prisons had decreased to 202%, from 214% in 2025.

articles.title: The 'unity' fight splitting Danielle Smith's party intensifies at UCP convention
articles.summary: Premier's loyalists and pro-independence activists campaigning for control of party's influential board of directors.

image.caption: With activists from both the separatist and moderate wings of their coalition, UCP conventions have been contentious throughout Danielle Smith's four years as leader. (Emmanuel Prince-Thauvette/Radio-Canada)

blocks.text: Loyalists to Premier Danielle Smith are spearheading massive get-out-the-vote efforts for this weekend’s UCP convention, in hopes of seizing firm control of the party board in the aftermath of Alberta’s separation referendum.
This includes offers to pay for meeting tickets and a surge of registrations by members from the party’s old Progressive Conservative wing, CBC News has learned.

On the other side, grassroots party activists are also spending money and organizing in hopes of electing more independence-friendly officials to the party board. But after several years of insurgent groups like Take Back Alberta holding sway at conventions, this could be the year that the party establishment strikes back.
“This is a similar effort that would happen for an actual leadership race,” one senior United Conservative told CBC News about the intensity of convention organizing.

However, Smith’s leadership isn’t up for a vote at this UCP annual general meeting, starting Friday in Calgary. It’s not the party president’s turn to be up for election either, but convention-goers will choose another eight of 18 voting directors on the UCP’s board, including chief financial officer and regional directors.
This weekend’s battle, insiders believe, could help tilt the board’s balance away from independence — or from the influence of Smith and her inner circle.
One party organizer trying to rally traditional Tories to the convention is Hal Danchilla, a lobbying firm partner who served as a key advisor to former premier Ralph Klein.
To explain his aims ahead of the convention, he hearkened back to the approach taken during the old Progressive Conservative dynasty, before its 2017 merger with the Wildrose Party to form the UCP.
“One of the fundamental pieces in the past was that we worked for the leader of the party,” Danchilla told CBC News. “The leader didn’t work for the party.”
At past UCP conventions, partisans have shown support for Smith. But they've also elected party board members that her loyalists are now trying to push out. (Jeff McIntosh/The Canadian Press)
How pitched are attempts to stack the convention, which a record 7,000 members are registered to attend?

One Tory in Calgary who hasn’t been active in the UCP told CBC News that of the many people who have urged her to attend this weekend, two separately offered to cover her registration fee, which after the early-bird discount runs $399.

The Tory, who spoke on the condition she not be named, declined the money, preferring to go on her own dime (and she wouldn’t say who offered). But the urgency got her concerned about the party’s health heading into next year’s provincial election.
“If you have to whip your own party like this at your own convention ... how are you going to run an election?” she said.
Multiple sources said the Smith loyalists’ goal is to bring thousands of supporters out to the convention, to outnumber activists’ efforts on the other side.
After 75 per cent of Albertans supported staying in Canada in the October referendum, the premier shifted from her long-standing tolerance for openly backing separatism within her UCP ranks.

She said she wants everyone speaking for her party to acknowledge and accept the referendum results, including all MLAs and election candidates next year. The party has issued a pledge for all board candidates and current riding association presidents to sign, saying they “abide by” that vote’s outcome — although several presidents have refused that demand.
New candidates for board posts include several UCPers who campaigned against a united Canada, including Chris Scott of the independence group Let’s Talk Alberta.

Other candidates have banded together on a slate dubbed Team Unity, including Patrick Malkin, a party vice-president whose day job is as the premier’s deputy chief of staff. This “team” professes loyalty to the premier and a commitment to a “strong Alberta within a United Canada.”

“It is eight like-minded, hard-working dedicated people who are running for the board that are unifying together,” Ken Engler, a candidate to be the party’s chief financial officer, said at a Calgary board candidates’ forum last week.
Part of an email sent to UCP members from board candidates calling themselves the party's 'Unity' slate. (United Conservative Party/CBC news graphic illustration)
The banner on this group’s campaign emails features the premier’s photo, but Smith has not endorsed any candidates.

“While the premier is not involved or associated with the creation of this group, it is great to see individual members from across our province organizing to keep our party united,” Smith spokesperson Ryan Fournier said in an email.

On Wednesday, a group of 21 Calgary business and community leaders sent party members a letter endorsing the slate's eight candidates to keep the "UCP strong and unified." It was co-ordinated by lawyer and veteran conservative fundraiser Brian Felesky, who said he backs Smith's efforts to "put the whole issue of separation to rest."
"I firmly believe in a united Canada, a united Alberta, and I don’t want this AGM to be hijacked," said another signatory, former Calgary police commission chair Mike Shaikh.

Not only is this slate taking on some of the pro-independence challengers like Scott — who willingly signed the post-referendum pledge — but it’s also running candidates against a few current directors with ties to the independence cause, including regional directors Brad LaForge and Mark Hunt, and CFO Jack Redekop.
“I don't need to be the establishment's choice, but I want to be your choice,” LaForge told the Calgary forum last Friday.
“I'm asking you to vote for the kind of party we can be, one where respect matters more than influence — where unity is something we build together, not something we demand from one another.”

The “unity” slate has also rankled the party’s board president, Rob Smith. In a social media post on Tuesday, he said it’s “extremely offensive” to suggest that other candidates aren’t for unity, and announced he’d endorse three contenders running against Team Unity members.
Danchilla’s view of the party working for the leader and not vice versa runs counter to the perspective of many UCP grassroots activists who prefer more of a bottom-up approach.

“The party doesn’t exist so that the leadership can use it to accomplish their goals,” Scott told CBC News this week. “The membership is supposed to be operating the party to make the leader and the government accomplish their goal.”

The party’s board will have particular importance with 2027 Alberta election looming. It holds influence over the UCP’s multimillion-dollar war chest and candidate selection, among other political matters.

Several current directors like LaForge and Hunt joined the board with the backing of activist groups like David Parker’s Take Back Alberta and Mitch Sylvestre’s pro-independence Alberta Prosperity Project, which sought to exert more heavy influence on the party and UCP government by controlling the board.

As those groups gained power at party conventions, those from the Tory side retreated or stopped coming. In the first post-referendum convention, there’s a big effort to bring them back into the fold to preserve the UCP as a staunchly federalist (and anti-separatist) party.

Elan MacDonald has helped reach out to hundreds of Tories and UCPers, urging them to come to the AGM. She was deputy chief of staff to former Tory premiers Ed Stelmach and Alison Redford — both of whom Danielle Smith opposed as Wildrose leader — but has emerged recently as a Smith backer, hosting a coffee party for the premier at her Edmonton house last July. MacDonald recently left a University of Alberta job to become a government-relations consultant.
“Conservatives are re-engaging with the UCP for this AGM because they see a small sliver of conservatives dictating an agenda that we don't share,” MacDonald said.
“We need a board that is very clear that this is not a separatist party. This is a broad-based conservative party that has broad-based conservative values.”
Elan MacDonald served as a key aide for two former Tory premiers, and is currently in government relations. (flyyeg.com)

Danchilla, who is working with MacDonald’s team, said the group is not offering to pay convention-goers. CBC was unable to confirm the identities of any organizations or individuals who are offering to cover costs of those intending to support the Unity slate.

On the other side of this board election battle, a pro-independence group named Next Step Alberta is offering to cover half the convention fees for like-minded supporters. Next Step head Nathan Steinke said he’s been getting referrals from APP to provide the subsidies to conservatives who bought their own tickets.

“I think that sovereignty-minded people need to be represented,” Steinke said. He’s a former UCP cabinet aide and is married to Samantha Steinke, a veteran party board member who he says has accompanied him to some events where he’s touted his project.
Sylvestre, who has told APP backers he wants to get 1,000 of them to the convention, confirmed Nathan Steinke’s group is supporting him, and said repaying ticket-holders is “completely aboveboard.”
While party members must register individually for the AGM, the rules do not prohibit covering others’ costs, party spokesperson Dave Prisco said in an email.
Nathan Steinke said his budget for the effort is modest — under $15,000 — and he’s so far financially supported fewer than 100 AGM attendees.
He said he’s worried about what happens to the UCP if independence activists are shut out from the board and separatists don’t feel they have a home in the party.
“You know, if the establishment basically rolls in … and just steamrolls us, then I think that they are in some ways damaging unity more than sovereignty ever could,” Steinke said.

'Canada Guy' stages a small counter-protest at an October independence rally at the Alberta legislature. UCP Leader Danielle Smith has urged her party to stop talking about separatism. (Amanda May Erickson/The Canadian Press)
Chris Scott, who is confident he has enough supporters to get elected as the party’s central region director, echoed this sentiment
“If the rural and the grassroots folks smell funny business, that’s going to be reflected in the election,” he said.
“I think the party has to be really careful about the image they portray to the members, because there’s a lot of members that already feel disenfranchised.”

Concern about the next election and the UCP’s reputation is very much on the minds of many key party figures. The NDP’s byelection win in a former safe Calgary seat in September surprised organizers throughout the UCP, and party president Rob Smith told one podcast recently about the lesson it sent.

“What our door-knockers are hearing, not just in the official Calgary-Shaw byelection, but in door-knocking that’s happening across the province: there are an awful lot of Albertans who believe the UCP is a separatist party,” he told the show Unfiltered earlier this month.

Some in the party are bidding to deputize several hundred or thousand convention attendees to help dispel that image, and notch a comfortable win for Danielle Smith in her final convention before next October’s election.

articles.title: ICE almost deported this Eritrean woman to a third country after Canada turned her away
articles.summary: Rahel Negassi is one of several asylum seekers who Canadian immigration lawyers say were erroneously denied entry into Canada and wound up in the murky, at times frightening world of ICE detention…

image.caption: Rahel Negassi spent two months in an ICE detention facility in Texas last year and was nearly deported to a third country after Canadian border agents denied her entry into Canada. She fought for a second chance and now lives in Kitchener, Ont., with her son. (Evan Mitsui/CBC)

blocks.text: Rahel Negassi was two months into her detention at a Texas Immigration Customs Enforcement (ICE) facility in September 2025. Earlier that summer, the Eritrean woman had tried to claim asylum at the Canadian border where she was turned away, and she was about to be deported to a third country.

Negassi fled Eritrea's authoritarian government in the late '90s as it was entering one of many wars with neighbouring Ethiopia, taking a winding path from Sudan to the U.K., before landing in the U.S. in 2003. She spent nearly a year in immigration detention before her asylum application was rejected when her siblings weren't available to vouch for her. She was released as a paroled undocumented migrant, which meant regular check-ins with ICE.

She moved to Michigan, studied nursing and had two children, a daughter, now 18, and a son, now 13. She lived in the U.S. for two decades without issue, under authorizations the U.S. government provided her to work as a nurse because they could not deport her to Eritrea.

But after Trump was re-elected, ICE began deportation proceedings and Negassi spent months preparing to move to Canada with her son. She gathered the necessary documents, including the results of a DNA test proving her connection to her brother in Canada. That qualified her for one of the few exceptions to Canada's Safe Third Country Agreement (STCA) with the U.S.
Negassi's case seemed, to her, so certain. She never thought they'd be turned away.

items: What is the Safe Third Country agreement?

blocks.text: "I was not scared. I thought: 'I already have the DNA test. More than DNA, what can you bring?'" Negassi told CBC in a recent interview from Kitchener, Ont., where she and her son now live.

Negassi, 51, is one of several asylum seekers who were erroneously denied entry into Canada, then wound up in the murky, at times frightening, world of ICE detention since U.S. President Donald Trump took office for his second term last year, according to Canadian lawyers who have taken on their cases.
Canadian border agents skeptical
When she arrived at the Canadian border on June 27, 2025, Negassi says border agents immediately expressed skepticism that she was really born in Eritrea.
"He said, 'Just tell me you are Ethiopian. I know you guys pretend to be Eritrean and you come to Canada and you ask asylum,'" Negassi said.

Then, at her official interview, she says the officer expressed doubt and called her brother to verify facts, but they had been separated for decades. When the agent returned, Negassi was informed she was being found ineligible to enter Canada. Even the DNA tests, approved by a company endorsed by the Canada Border Services Agency, weren't enough.

items: 2 families rejected at Canadian border are now mired in what lawyer calls a 'black hole' of ICE detention

blocks.text: She spent four or five days in a detention facility at the U.S. border with her son before they were separated — he went to live with his stepfather, a U.S. citizen. Negassi was ushered onto a flight bound for an ICE detention centre in El Valle, Texas.
Her husband contacted Ottawa-based immigration lawyer Heather Neufeld as soon as he found out the two had been detained.
Heather Neufeld, an Ottawa immigration lawyer, represented Negassi and helped push for her case to be reconsidered at the Canadian border last year. (Ousama Farag/CBC)
Lawyers challenge border agreement

Neufeld has overseen many cases similar to Negassi's. She's part of a team of lawyers representing a constitutional challenge to the STCA, which bars most asylum seekers from entering Canada through the U.S.

According to statistics the team cited in Federal Court earlier this month, at least 4,323 people were found ineligible to enter Canada and were returned to the U.S. between Jan. 1, 2025 and March 30, 2026. One-fifth of them were children.

items: Federal Court challenge says Canada failing to protect refugees turned back to U.S.

blocks.text: "The percentage of people who would manage to access counsel on these turn-back cases is minuscule," Neufeld told CBC News. "All the rest of these people … are just summarily deported."

On behalf of Amnesty International Canada, the Canadian Council for Refugees and the Canadian Council of Churches, the lawyers argue the STCA violates equality rights under section 15 of the Canadian Charter because it disproportionately harms vulnerable groups, such as racialized people, women, children and 2SLGBTQ+ individuals.
They say those groups, namely women fleeing gender violence and 2SLGBTQ+ people, are overlooked by U.S. asylum law and face harrowing conditions and family separations in immigration detention.
How ICE detention is forcing immigrants out of the U.S.

Though that was also the case under previous U.S. administrations, Julia Sande, a lawyer specializing in privacy and migrant rights at Amnesty International Canada says "things are so much worse right now," making the constitutional challenge even more urgent.

What's more, Canadian border agents do not appear to be informing asylum claimants that they may qualify to come to Canada if they can prove they face personal dangers, such as death, extreme sanction, inhumane treatment or a real risk of forced deportation, without evaluation in the U.S. These "safety valves" are listed in a 2023 Supreme Court decision on the STCA's constitutionality.
Sande says this process is opaque and not publicly available. "It's not clear to anyone, let alone an unrepresented refugee showing up at the border, what on Earth you would need to do," she said.

items: How ICE detention is forcing immigrants out of the U.S.

blocks.text: Lawyers representing the federal government have argued that the claims presented in the constitutional challenge are moot, because most of the asylum claimants cited now have status in Canada.

In response to a request for comment, a spokesperson for Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada said the border agreement "is designed to keep the Canada–U.S. border safe and well-managed. It helps avoid sudden spikes in asylum claims that could overwhelm border crossings, housing, and processing systems."
Negassi says it took her months to recover from her time at an ICE detention centre in Texas last year. (Evan Mitsui/CBC)
One of the lucky ones
Negassi says she was one of the lucky ones.

After Neufeld filed a request for judicial review of Negassi's case in the summer of 2025, the Canadian Department of Justice arranged for ICE to have her sent back to the Canadian border on Sept. 2, 2025.
Negassi says her earlier optimism was replaced by the cold fear of being turned away by Canada again. However, this time, when she was accompanied by Neufeld, she was let in.
"When they say the United States is safe … the United States is not safe for anybody at this time," she said.
"It was bad. It was so bad," Negassi said of her border experience and being detained by ICE, which she says transported her back in time to her journey to flee Eritrea.

items: Shackled, abused and humiliated: Report paints grim picture of life in ICE detention

blocks.text: "You are in fight or flight. You do everything — your energy, everything — just to survive," Negassi said, recalling both her experience as a young asylum seeker and, then again last year.

She's been working to obtain her Canadian nursing licence and says she's only now recovering from the ordeal. Still, she says she's grateful to have made it to Canada with her son and once again feels safe and is rebuilding her life.
"I want to show Canadians, everybody — you see, I made it," she said. "I'm still OK. The United States didn't break me."
Negassi, who is Pentecostal Christian, has been advocating for human rights causes in her home country of Eritrea from abroad. (Evan Mitsui/CBC)

articles.title: The threat of Starlink looms over Quebecor's Telus bid. But are Canadian telecoms actually vulnerable?
articles.summary: In Quebecor’s $31-billion bid to take over Telus, the theme of Canadian sovereignty is emerging front and centre as the Montreal company pitches a merger, in part, to battle the threat of American…

image.caption: The silhouette of Elon Musk and Starlink logo are seen in this illustration taken June 11, 2026. (Dado Ruvic/Reuters)

blocks.text: In Quebecor’s $31-billion bid to take over Telus, the theme of Canadian sovereignty is emerging front and centre as the Montreal company pitches a merger, in part, to battle the threat of American satellite companies like Elon Musk's SpaceX.

But some researchers and critics say those services, particularly the company's Starlink satellite internet subsidiary, are not the threat to traditional Canadian telecoms that Quebecor CEO Pierre Karl Péladeau says it is.

In a Sunday interview with CBC’s Rosemary Barton, Péladeau framed the proposal as a sovereignty measure, noting that Starlink is likely looking to expand its operations. He likened it to Netflix, which he said massively impacted the Canadian broadcasting industry despite not having a licence with the Canadian Radio-television and Telecommunications Commission.

"If someone thinks that the Starlink business model is to service only some people in Arkansas, they're completely wrong. Their business model is the world, like Netflix's business model was the world," Péladeau said.
"So I think we should inspire our thinking and our mindset according, you know, [to] the mistakes we did regarding broadcasting and we know what is the cost for Canadians to be invaded."
What would a Quebecor-Telus merger mean for your phone bill?
Still, Dwayne Winseck, director of the Global Media and Internet Concentration Project, is cautious of that framing, calling Péladeau’s remarks "rhetorical distractions."

He noted that while Starlink Mobile, SpaceX’s satellite-to-mobile service, aims to expand in the U.S., it isn’t close to competing with the big three carriers in the US — AT&T, T-Mobile and Verizon — which also oppose its cellular ambitions.
And in Canada, SpaceX has stated it does not intend to compete with Canadian telecoms, but rather work with them.
‘Sovereignty challenge is real’
Last week, Quebecor announced it had made a proposal worth $31 billion to take over Telus.

Telus is currently reviewing an enhanced proposal submitted by Quebecor earlier this month, but its leadership has said it has "serious concerns" about whether regulators would ever approve shrinking the telecommunications market.

Based in Montreal, Quebecor is Canada's fourth-largest telecom company. In recent years it has boomed in value since acquiring Freedom Mobile in 2023, and using its competitors' networks to provide mobile service to customers.

Last week, Prime Minister Mark Carney said that under certain circumstances and depending on the market structure, an oligopoly can lead to more competition with fewer players. He did not comment directly on the Quebecor proposal.

items: Quebecor CEO defends Telus bid, cites falling wireless prices and Canada's sovereignty

blocks.text: "Telecom assets are strategic for our country — we all know this. And then therefore, we need to make sure that we're going to be on the same footing," Péladeau told CBC.

With the recent push for more Canadian independence, the idea of supporting domestic businesses has become "so sensible and part of everyday conversation," said David Nieborg, a media professor at the University of Toronto.
He added that there’s a sense that Ottawa has typically been protective of certain industries, like telecoms, shielding Canadian companies from foreign conglomerates.

David Nieborg is a professor of media and platform studies at the University of Toronto. He says a Canadian push for sovereignty makes sense, but in telecommunications, it can be a costly trade-off for consumers. (Submitted by David Nieborg)

Nieborg said he understands the logic of the sovereignty argument. But, he said, "that's the trade-off that has an impact on pricing on Canadian data, and Canadian telecommunication has been notoriously expensive."

"Sovereignty and innovation and competition should not necessarily be at odds with each other," Nieborg said. "The sovereignty challenge is real, but at the very same time it comes at a significant cost, I think, to Canadian consumers."
What is Starlink's reach in Canada?

SpaceX introduced Starlink to Canadians in late 2020, providing an option for low-latency internet service, particularly for remote or rural communities. It later brought Starlink Mobile coverage in 2025, through a partnership with Rogers.

Earlier this year, SpaceX told Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada (ISED) that it would offer Starlink Mobile to every interested Canadian carrier, but "Starlink does not plan to offer its own standalone service nor does it plan to deal exclusively with any one carrier."
In July 2025, Rogers trialled Rogers Satellite, a texting and light-data service carried by Starlink satellites. The company took it commercial last December.

Dwayne Winseck is a professor at Carleton University’s School of Journalism and Communication and director of the Global Media and Internet Concentration Project. He says Quebecor's sovereignty argument is 'speculation heaped on speculation.' (Submitted by Dwayne Winseck)
Starlink's potential threat to telecoms is "speculation heaped upon speculation," said Winseck, who tracks communication, internet and media markets in Canada and dozens of other countries.
He noted that the U.S. company is not competing in the same arena as Canadian telecoms providers — rather, it is primarily serving a niche market where the big players are not.

As of 2025, Winseck's research shows Starlink is Canada's fifth largest internet service provider by revenue and sixth largest by subscribers; it only holds about five per cent of internet access revenue in Canada.

"Incumbents ... have failed to serve rural, remote, far north and Indigenous communities for decades and up to a century," Winseck said. "And what does Elon Musk do? Well, he swoops in and provides a service that people really desperately need."

In 2025, SpaceX announced Starlink had over half a million customers across Canada. The country has become its fifth largest market, according to Ookla Research’s 2025 global satellite broadband performance report.
The case for sovereignty

Still, Canada is looking to break Starlink's grip on Arctic military communications, as Ottawa-based defence technology company Dominion Dynamics recently struck a deal with Canadian satellite giant Telesat to develop a homegrown alternative to Starlink’s military variant, Starshield.
In an interview with the New York Times last week, Carney pointed to disruptions in Starshield’s connectivity in Ukraine as motivation.

"You can't unsee that once you've seen it, particularly given the integration of space technology and defence technology," he said. "The issue for us, the issue for the Koreans, the issue for the Japanese, the issue for the Europeans is can we build, at a minimum, a redundant system or a sovereign system?"
Carney wants Canada to move away from Elon Musk’s Starlink. Can it? | Hanomansing Tonight

Rob McMahon, associate media and technology studies professor at the University of Alberta, said that Starlink is so concentrated in certain parts of the country that it doesn't pose much of a threat to Canadian telecoms outside those particular regions.

"Sometimes this discourse of sovereignty could be leveraged as a way to support the increasing … concentration of ownership and mergers and so on, whereas I don't really see Starlink in that way," he said.

In an emailed statement to CBC News, Péladeau said, "What matters for Canada is not what any one foreign company intends to do today, but whether the country retains control over critical communications infrastructure in the long term."

articles.title: EU leaders brace for tough talks on budget and Ukraine – Europe live
articles.summary:
António Costa says the next long-term budget is ‘the most important’ item on the agenda

Sweden’s Ulf Kristersson suggested the talks could even go beyond December and into 2027, as…

blocks.text: Morning opening: EU leaders meet for talks on budget, Ukraine

blocks.caption: Jakub Krupa

blocks.text: Jakub Krupa
EU leaders are meeting in Brussels today and tomorrow for tricky talks on the next financial budget and Ukraine, with disagreements threatening to expose deep divisions within the bloc.

The European Council president, António Costa, told reporters this morning that the next long-term budget was “the most important” item on the agenda, as he acknowledged that getting an agreement at this summit may not be possible.
“My objective is to bring our leader closer to a deal,” he said, adding he is hoping that a compromise could be agreed “by the end of this year.”

blocks.caption: European Council president António Costa arrives at the Europa building ahead of a meeting of the European Council in Brussels, Belgium. Photograph: Olivier Hoslet/EPA

blocks.text: Arrivals are now under way and I will bring you some reactions from the leaders coming in for the meeting.
Spain’s Pedro Sánchez is the only leader not present as he is fighting for his political survival ahead of this Sunday’s parliamentary election. France’s Emmanuel Macron will represent his views.

Elsewhere, I will keep an eye on the latest news coming from Ukraine and on Serbia, where we are expecting a date for the presidential election – also by the end of the year – to choose Aleksandar Vučić’s successor.
It’s Thursday, 26 November 2026, it’s Jakub Krupa here, and this is Europe Live.
Good morning.
Key events

items: 2m agoUkraine 'probably will face a winter like hell,' Estonia's PM warns, as he calls for no cuts to EU budget
21m agoMorning opening: EU leaders meet for talks on budget, Ukraine
21m agoWatch out for clash on cohesion funds, Ukraine support
21m agoSweden's Kristersson suggests budget talks could drag beyond December

blocks.text: Ukraine 'probably will face a winter like hell,' Estonia's PM warns, as he calls for no cuts to EU budget
Estonia’s Kristen Michal argued against any cuts to the EU budget, “because if we look at what Russia is doing on the eastern border, [it] needs protecting; needs investments and money.”
He also warned that Ukraine “probably will face a winter like hell,” and so “they must know that Ukraine has its back, with money and everything we have.”
“They should not … be in a position [that they need] to take a bad deal.”
Michal said that there are “no signs that Putin wants peace,” with Russia trying “mind games” of pretending that the European security architecture poses any threat to Moscow.
“The European security architecture was fine until Putin attacked Ukraine,” he said.
He also disagreed with the Czech suggestion that the issues of EU budget and Ukraine should not be linked.
“Europe and Ukraine are linked, because Ukraine is fighting for us. We are only counting euros, and that is not a bad thing, … but they are shedding blood. So, whatever we can do, we must,” he said.
Sweden's Kristersson suggests budget talks could drag beyond December
Sweden’s Ulf Kristersson suggested the talks could even go beyond December and into 2027, as with the budget kicking in only in 2028, “we aren’t in that hurry.”
He said the leaders should see December as “a target or a goal,” but not as “the deadline.”
“I think you can’t simply say that we are will accept a budget we don’t believe in simply because we have a deadline in December 2026.” He added:
“But of course we need to finalise it sooner or later so I don’t mind finding a sound and reasonable compromise in December, but we are not there yet.”

But Kristersson pointedly backed Germany’s Merz against the four central eastern European countries, saying “it is not acceptable to simply kidnap [the issue of support for] Ukraine” by saying “we will accept the EU support for Ukraine, but we will not pay for it ourselves.”
“I don’t think that is a reasonable way of thinking, not in accordance with the basic rules for the European Council. We should not make opt out a new tradition, that’s my strong belief,” he said.
Watch out for clash on cohesion funds, Ukraine support

One thing to watch is what happens with four countries that do not particularly want to contribute to the EU’s next round of financing for Ukraine, and focus on keeping cohesion funds for their communities.

blocks.caption: Czech prime minister Andrej Babiš speaks to the media as he attends a European Union special summit in Brussels, Belgium. Photograph: Yves Herman/Reuters

blocks.text: Bulgaria, Czech Republic, Hungary and Slovakia remain opposed, and German chancellor Friedrich Merz leads the group that wants to pressure them into agreement by linking the new budget with funds for Ukraine, threatening to veto the financial settlement if needed.
Czech PM Andrej Babiš argued this morning saying such solution was “not possible” under the treaties.
He said that maintaining high cohesion spending was a priority for his government, as “we don’t have a highway to Austria and we have to build our hospitals.”
“Financing of Ukraine should be negotiated separately, and the most important [thing] is the life of our citizens,” he said.
Asked if he’s expecting a deal by the end of the year, he noted that the positions are “so different, we will see.”

articles.title: Two screenings of Pakistani TV show cancelled in India after backlash
articles.summary: The show, Dar-e-Nijaat, has become a sensation in India but is now embroiled in a political row.

blocks.text: Until Wednesday, the weekend plans of some television enthusiasts in the Indian city of Bengaluru involved dressing up, having an elaborate dinner and finding out what happens next in the lives of a wildly popular fictional Pakistani couple.
Then geopolitics intervened.

Two private screenings of Dar-e-Nijaat (Door to Salvation), a Pakistani television drama that has become something of a sensation on Indian social media, were called off after an online backlash and police scrutiny.
The serial, which airs on Pakistan's ARY Digital, is available to Indian viewers through some YouTube channels, though the broadcaster's official channel is blocked in India.

The controversy comes amid a renewed appetite for Pakistani entertainment in India, even though cultural engagement remains a sensitive issue following a brief but intense military confrontation between the two nuclear-armed neighbours in May last year.
A similar gathering in Delhi, featuring quizzes and even a virtual interaction with the show's director, had already divided opinion online last week.

In Bengaluru, one screening, scheduled for Saturday at a restaurant, offered a Persian and Arabic dinner alongside two episodes of the serial for a small ticket charge. The other - scheduled at a private theatre and meant only for family members - asked guests to dress in their "best Pakistani ensemble".
As promotional posters circulated online, several social media users questioned the appropriateness of such gatherings and called for police intervention. Both events have since been called off.
The backlash has coincided with calls to block the release of another Pakistani drama in India.

The All Indian Cine Workers Association (AICWA) has written to Prime Minister Narendra Modi demanding that Netflix's upcoming Pakistani series, Jo Bachay Hain Sang Samait Lo (Gather whatever is left), be barred from release in India.
Featuring Fawad Khan, Mahira Khan, Sanam Saeed and other stars with many Indian fans, the series is Pakistan's first Netflix original. Its global premiere is scheduled for 4 December.

In its letter to Modi on Tuesday, the AICWA argued that releasing the series in India would disregard the sentiments of families affected by terrorism. India has long accused Pakistan of supporting cross-border terrorism, an allegation Islamabad denies.
The association has also sought permanent legislation prohibiting Pakistani entertainment content in India. Netflix is yet to clarify whether the series will be available to Indian subscribers.
The developments have revived an old debate in India over whether cultural ties with Pakistan should be kept separate from political differences.
India and Pakistan share a rich cultural heritage, but relations between them have often been fraught since they were carved out of British India as independent nations in 1947.

And cultural exchanges have often been among the first casualties of political tensions. Pakistani ghazal singers with devoted audiences in India have periodically found themselves unable to perform there. Indian films, immensely popular in Pakistan, have disappeared from its cinemas. Artistic collaborations have flourished during periods of relative calm, only to unravel when tensions flare again.

The early 2010s were a particularly fertile period. Pakistani singers Atif Aslam and Rahat Fateh Ali Khan were among the most recognisable voices in Hindi cinema. The launch of the television channel Zindagi in 2014 brought Pakistani serials into Indian living rooms, introducing viewers to stories whose language and emotional worlds were familiar, but whose treatment of everyday life often felt refreshingly different.

By 2016, Fawad Khan was appearing in some of Bollywood's most prominent productions. But attacks on Indian security forces in Uri that year and in Pulwama in 2019, both of which India blamed on Pakistan-based militant groups, narrowed the space for cultural collaboration. Pakistan - which has constantly denied any involvement - also imposed restrictions on Indian entertainment.
Even as formal exchanges dwindled, Pakistani dramas found new audiences in India on YouTube, while music continued to travel across the border through streaming platforms.
But the events of last year disrupted even this relatively informal relationship.

On 22 April 2025, militants killed 26 people, most of them tourists, in Pahalgam in Indian-administered Kashmir. India blamed Pakistan-linked militants; Islamabad denied involvement. In May, India launched military strikes on what it described as terrorist infrastructure in Pakistan and Pakistan-administered Kashmir. Four days of fighting followed before a ceasefire was announced.
Amid widespread anger in India, the government asked streaming platforms to discontinue Pakistani-origin content, while social media accounts of several Pakistani celebrities were blocked.

Fawad Khan's much-anticipated return to Hindi cinema with Abir Gulaal was thwarted when the film was denied permission for release in India. Criticism of India's military action by Pakistani artistes fuelled further anger.

For much of the past year, Indian audiences have encountered Pakistan on screen largely through the prism of national security. In December, millions flocked to watch Dhurandhar, Aditya Dhar's espionage thriller, whose success inspired a fascination with the gangsters, spies and political intrigues of Karachi.
But in recent months, a more familiar kind of fascination with Pakistan has begun to resurface.
Pakistani songs like Alfaaz have become hugely popular on Indian social media, while Dar-e-Nijaat, a story about marriage, heartbreak and domestic life, has found an enthusiastic audience.

Written by the celebrated Urdu novelist Umera Ahmed, the serial revolves around the marriage of Zaryab (Durefishan Saleem), a young woman recovering from a romantic betrayal, and Abu Bakar (Sheheryar Munawar), a deeply religious man.

Though the drama explores questions of faith and redemption, it is Abu Bakar's tenderness towards his wife that has earned him perhaps the highest accolade in the contemporary vocabulary of courtship: a "green flag".
It was this enthusiasm for the drama that prompted the organiser of one of the screenings in Bengaluru to plan an event at a private theatre in her apartment complex.
What she had envisaged as a small family gathering, she said, had been interpreted quite differently once the invitation found its way onto X.
"My family was saying why should we cancel?" she said. But ultimately, she decided to call it off.

articles.title: Labor group decries AirAsia's layoff of 90 pilots amid union drive
articles.summary: The Trade Union Congress of the Philippines has called for a congressional probe into AirAsia Philippines' decision to lay off about 90 pilots, saying termination notices went out on the same day the…

blocks.text: November 26, 2026 | 4:28pm

An AirAsia passenger plane takes for Malaysia for the first time since the route was reopened after being suspended for almost three years due to the COVID-19 pandemic, at Sultan Iskandar Muda International Airport in Blang Bintang, Aceh province on Oct. 3, 2022.
AFP / Chaideer Mahyuddin

MANILA, Philippines — The Trade Union Congress of the Philippines has called for a congressional probe into AirAsia Philippines' decision to lay off about 90 pilots, saying termination notices went out on the same day the pilots' union received an order clearing the way for a certification election.

The budget carrier — in a statement by general manager and president Anna Victoria Lu — has announced that sustained high jet fuel prices and unfavorable exchange rates have driven up its operating costs and forced it to cut routes and flight frequencies, thereby reducing the number of staff needed.
The affected captains and first officers were told their employment would end on December 31.
According to the labor group, the pilots who would be retrenched account for nearly half of the roughly 200 pilots that the AirAsia Philippines Pilots Union is seeking to represent.
'No ordinary coincidence,' says labor group TUCP

The union of AirAsia pilots filed its petition for a certification election on September 4. A certification election is a secret ballot in which workers decide which union, if any, will represent them in collective bargaining with management.
The Department of Labor and Employment granted the petition in an order dated November 19, according to the union, which reportedly received the order on November 25.
By then, the layoffs were already in motion, as management announced a workforce reduction at a meeting with pilots on November 24, according to a union advisory.
"This is no ordinary coincidence that can simply be brushed aside as a management decision. It demands answers," TUCP said in its statement.

"No one, especially our AirAsia pilots, should be forced to spend Christmas and welcome the New Year with no job just because they dared to organize and assert their right to collective bargaining," the labor group added.
TUCP asked the airline to suspend the retrenchments, keep all affected pilots employed and "sit down" with the union "in good faith."
It also called on DOLE to act and cited the human rights policy of the parent company, Malaysia-based AirAsia Group Berhad, which lists labor rights among its commitments on its website.
The union is set to file a notice of strike Thursday.
Job cuts necessary, says AirAsia
AirAsia Philippines in its statement described the job cuts as "a very difficult decision" made "to ensure the long-term stability of the airline."
It said it recognized the impact on affected employees and their families and would support them "with care and transparency" through the transition.
The layoffs follow months of financial strain on AirAsia's Philippine unit and its parent after Jet fuel prices climbed sharply due to the conflict in the Middle East.
In October, the Court of Appeals dismissed the airline's petition to cancel the registration of a pilots' labor group, the AirAsia Philippines Pilot Association.
The court rejected the company's argument that pilots are managerial employees barred from joining unions.
Under Article 298 of the Labor Code, an employer may retrench workers to prevent business losses.

It must notify both the affected employees and DOLE in writing at least one month in advance, and pay separation pay of one month's salary or half a month's pay for every year of service, whichever is higher.

articles.title: Security guards are public figures in libel cases — Supreme Court
articles.summary: The Supreme Court has declared that security guards are considered "public figures" in matters concerning their professional conduct, placing them within the scope of qualified privileged…

blocks.text: November 26, 2026 | 4:23pm

MANILA, Philippines — The Supreme Court has declared that security guards are considered "public figures" in matters concerning their professional conduct, placing them within the scope of qualified privileged communication in libel cases.

The high court, in its August 2026 ruling penned by Supreme Court Associate Justice Marvic Leonen, made this clarification as it acquitted a barangay captain and a managing editor of criminal libel, reversing their previous convictions by the Regional Trial Court and the Court of Appeals.
The consolidated cases stemmed from two articles published in September 2014 in the tabloids Hataw and Police Files.
The articles were authored by Ligaya Santos, who was then serving as a barangay captain in Manila. Gloria Galuno, the managing editor of Hataw, was also charged.
The complainant, Alvin Velasquez, was a security officer and detachment commander of Tower A at the Gotesco Twin Tower Condominium.
Santos wrote the articles heavily criticizing Velasquez, calling him "barumbado" (ill-mannered), "arogante" (arrogant), "bastos" (rude), and "hunghang" (foolish).
The dispute arose when Santos summoned Velasquez to the barangay hall to settle a complaint filed by a condominium employee.
Velasquez refused the invitation and stood his ground, prohibiting his subordinate from leaving his post without an official subpoena.
Irked by the refusal, Santos published the columns, prompting Velasquez to file libel charges after claiming that the articles damaged his reputation and cost him a promotion.
While the prosecution argued that Velasquez was a private individual and therefore shielded from such public scrutiny, the Supreme Court disagreed.
Ruling
The high court ruled that a private complainant's status does not automatically exclude them from being considered a "public personage".
Citing jurisprudence, the high court said that a public figure includes anyone who adopts a profession or calling that gives the public a legitimate interest in their doings, affairs, and character.

“There is no denying that Velasquez is not a public official. However, by virtue of his profession as a security guard, the Court deems that he is considered a public figure due to his direct interaction with the public," the high court said.

"Security guards, by nature of their role, engage with the public daily and are entrusted with the responsibility of safeguarding lives and property. Their position inherently involves a level of public exposure, which justifies treating them as public figures in matters related to their professional conduct,” it added.

Because Velasquez was deemed a public figure involved in a matter of public interest, the articles written about him are protected under the doctrine of fair comment and classified as qualified privileged communication, according to the Supreme Court.

For a public figure to successfully prosecute someone for libel, the burden of proof shifts to the prosecution to prove "actual malice," meaning the author made the statement knowing it was false or with reckless disregard for whether it was false.
The Supreme Court found that the prosecution "miserably failed" to prove actual malice.

The high court noted that Santos's use of unflattering words like "barumbado" and "bastos" were merely expressions of her opinion, reasonably inferred from Velasquez's refusal to cooperate with barangay authorities.

“While the Court does not condone the use of foul language, the terms used to describe Velasquez are simply expressions of the author's opinion, reasonably inferred from the situation. As such, the statements unquestionably qualify as qualified privileged communication and can be actionable only if proven to have been made with actual malice,” the Supreme Court said.
Chilling effect
In the decision, the Supreme Court also reiterated its concerns over the "chilling effect" of criminal libel, especially in the digital age, where casual commentary can easily be penalized.

The Court emphasized that the state's interest in protecting individual reputations is better served through civil liabilities, such as damages under the Civil Code, rather than the "heavy hand of the State" and the threat of imprisonment.
"Unlike criminal libel, which threatens imprisonment and exerts a chilling effect on speech, civil remedies focus on repairing harm rather than punishing expression," the Court said.

According to the high court, existing libel laws are increasingly wielded by those with financial means to intimidate critics rather than genuinely repair reputational damage, creating a chilling effect in which people stay silent because of the prohibitive cost of defending themselves in court.

“In its present form, libel law operates less as a genuine mechanism for redressing reputational harm and more as a coercive means of deterring speech. Its use as an instrument of intimidation is particularly concerning when employed by those with the means to initiate legal action, thereby distorting the balance that the Constitution seeks to maintain. The result is a regime where individuals are discouraged from speaking out, not because their speech is unlawful, but because the cost of defending it is too high,” the high court said.

articles.title: Marcos: 29M coconut trees out of 100M target planted so far
articles.summary: President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. said Thursday that the administration has so far planted 29 million coconut trees out of its 100 million goal by the end of his term.

blocks.text: Published November 26, 2026 4:21pm
President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. said Thursday that the administration has so far planted 29 million coconut trees out of its 100 million goal by the end of his term.
Marcos witnessed the signing of a memorandum of understanding (MOU) for a 10-million coconut tree partnership with private-sector partners.
This is to help replace aging coconut trees by providing 10 million quality seeds to 100,000 smallholder farms in Mindanao.

“As of October this year, we have planted nearly 29 million coconut palms. Reaching our goal of 100 million is not going to be an easy task, but it is worth the effort. And an effort of this scale calls for the participation of everyone, of course, including the private sector,” Marcos said in his speech in Malacañang Palace.
The President said that a large number of the country’s coconut trees were aging, with many of them planted by previous generations.

“Many of our farmers still harvest from palms that their parents and grandparents once tended. Many coconut palms in the country have already reached an age that its productivity has begun to decline,” Marcos said.
Following the President’s speech, Marcos and Agriculture Secretary Francisco "Kiko" P. Tiu Laurel Jr. presented symbolic coconut palms to two indigenous farmer beneficiaries.

Among the signatories were Philippine Coconut Authority (PCA), Metro Pacific Agro Ventures, Inc., Vita Coco Community Foundation, Century Pacific Food, Inc. (CPFI) and HOPE. The President thanked the groups for focusing on Mindanao, which accounted for more than 60% of the country’s coconut production.
Marcos said that every coconut palm that will be planted is accounted for and will be reported on HOPE’s website.
The 100 million coconut tree target has been a longtime goal for Marcos. He reiterated this goal in his 2026 State of the Nation Address. —AOL, GMA News
