articles.title: Desperate appeals from women on death row in Iran after protests
articles.summary: Female protesters and dissidents are being sentenced to death in numbers not seen for decades, a rights group says.

blocks.text: Image source, Supplied by family
Twin sisters Romina (left) and Taraneh Rahimi were arrested in late January, their cousin says
ByBy Soroush Pakzad
BBC News Persian
Taraneh Rahimi is on death row in Iran.
In recent weeks, the 21-year-old has been unable to walk properly after her legs were beaten, and an ear-infection caused by an untreated head injury has affected her balance, her cousin says.
She is "keeping her spirits up" but "there are days she breaks down in tears," Masoud Nourmohammadi tells BBC News Persian.
He says Taraneh and her twin sister Romina were arrested after joining the anti-government protests that swept the country in January.

When the twins' mother first saw them in prison, their faces were so swollen and bruised, and their hair pulled out, that she could only recognise them by their voices, Nourmohammadi says, speaking from the US.
He says Taraneh signed a confession after interrogators threatened that her sister would be raped in front of her.
Taraneh is one of six women who have been sentenced to death this year in connection with the January protests, according to the UN's human rights rapporteur for Iran, Mai Sato.

The figure for men is much higher. However, women protesters and dissidents are being sentenced to death in numbers not seen for decades, as part of a "horrific rise" in politically motivated executions, Amnesty International's Iran researcher Raha Bahreini says.

blocks.caption: Image caption, January's protests began over economic grievances and spread to become Iran's largest since the 1979 Islamic Revolution

blocks.text: Image source, Anonymous/Getty Images
January's protests began over economic grievances and spread to become Iran's largest since the 1979 Islamic Revolution
The Iranian embassy in London told the BBC that claims of an increase in the use of the death penalty in protest-related cases were "misleading".

It categorically rejected allegations of the use of torture and any allegations that the death penalty has been imposed solely for peaceful protest, which it said is a "legitimate, and protected right".

It said death sentences in relation to the "riot in January 2026" were issued in cases involving "intentional murder" or "Moharebeh (the taking up of weapons with the intent to threaten or wreck the people's lives or property)".
The twins were seized in late January, Nourmohammadi says.

It was two weeks after the end of the protests, which began in late December over economic grievances and grew to become Iran's largest against the clerical establishment since the 1979 Islamic Revolution.

The US-based Human Rights Activists News Agency (Hrana) says it has identified more than 7,000 people killed in the crackdown that followed, most of them protesters, but believes the true figure is much higher.

The Iranian government accuses the US and Israel of fomenting the unrest, blaming "terrorists" and "rioters" for the deaths, which it says totalled 3,117 including some members of the security forces.

The twins' family did not find out where they were being held for more than three months, their cousin says. They were tried over protests in Isfahan, in an area of the city where a member of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) security force was killed.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Taraneh loves horses and would like to set up her own breeding centre one day, her cousin says

blocks.text: Image source, Instagram
Taraneh loves horses and would like to set up her own breeding centre one day, her cousin says

Court documents have not been published, but the BBC has seen part of a sentencing document which says Taraneh was convicted of moharebeh, which is a capital offence under Iran's Islamic Penal Code. The offence included "drawing a bladed weapon with the intent to endanger people's lives", according to the document.
Romina was sentenced to 25 years in jail for the lesser charge of aiding and abetting moharebeh, according to Sato, the UN rapporteur.

Nourmohammadi, who has been in contact with relatives and others in Iran familiar with the case, says both women deny all the charges against them and that there is no evidence Taraneh had a "bladed weapon".
Sato says the sisters were part of a case in which 10 people were sentenced to death, but that there was "no clarification of the acts attributed to each individual".

According to sources familiar with the case, the twins' lawyers have submitted a complaint alleging they were tortured and sexually abused during interrogation, but the investigation into it is being overseen by an official they accuse of torture.

blocks.caption: Image caption, This image of Mahboubeh Shabani, sentenced to death in September, has been shared with human rights groups

blocks.text: Image source, Supplied to human rights groups
This image of Mahboubeh Shabani, sentenced to death in September, has been shared with human rights groups
Voice messages from other women on death row contain a mixture of desperation and defiance.
Mahboubeh Shabani - widely reported to be 33 and a civil engineer - was sentenced to death in September under Iran's espionage law after transporting injured protesters, according to rights groups.

She called for help for herself and other prisoners from jail in the city of Mashhad in north-eastern Iran: "Everyone is in a terrible place mentally, especially those whose sentences have been finalised," she said.

Also jailed in Mashhad is Najmeh Amini, reported to be 23, who was initially arrested in the wake of the January protests, and later sentenced to death after being convicted of committing blasphemy in a social media post, according to rights groups.
"As long as I am alive, I have one hope, and that is to see a free and prosperous Iran before my life ends by the noose," a voice message attributed to her says.

In addition, Mojdeh Hashemi Bazargani - reported to be aged 27 - is also facing execution, according to rights groups. They say she was convicted of charges including "espionage", after being arrested in April, during the current war between Iran and Israel and the US.
The US-based Iranian rights group Tavaana has shared audio it says is of a phone call she made from prison, describing being beaten in the head, neck and body and made to sign a confession.
The woman in the recording says: "They accused me of espionage. They say you've been paid for it. If I had been paid for espionage, I would have a car or a house. I have nothing."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Najmeh Amini has been sentenced to death after being convicted of committing blasphemy in a social media post, rights groups say

blocks.text: Image source, Supplied to Hrana
Najmeh Amini has been sentenced to death after being convicted of committing blasphemy in a social media post, rights groups say
Amnesty International describes the charges in all three of these cases and also the twins as "politically motivated".

In response to the BBC's questions, the Iranian Embassy in London said "any allegations of the use of torture in connection with the mentioned cases are categorically rejected". It did not comment further on individual cases, but said "confessions obtained under duress have no legal validity".
At least 39 people have already been executed in connection with the January protests, according to Sato.

She notes a "sharp" increase in arrests and sentences across both men and women, and sees the rise in death sentences for women as an "escalation and expansion" of an "established pattern of repression".
Iranian human rights lawyer Musa Barzin, who is based in Turkey, says "it appears that factors such as gender or age now carry less weight in determining the severity of punishment".
Official detail on cases is often scant and some may go unreported.

However, Sato says as well as the six women she identified as being arrested in connection with protests, a further three have received death sentences this year - for "blasphemy" and "corruption on Earth charges, in relation to the war in March" and "espionage and moharebeh".
In comparison, these nine sentences are more than Hrana recorded for women for similar offences over the whole decade to 2025 - with no more than three in any one year.

The death sentences in three of the cases Sato identified as being linked to the protests have since been overturned – though two of those have been sent for retrial. She says she is concerned by an "increasingly frequent pattern" where overturned death sentences are later "reimposed by a parallel branch of the judiciary once public attention has subsided".

blocks.caption: Image caption, Taraneh (left) and Romina both say they gave baseless confessions after being tortured

blocks.text: Taraneh (left) and Romina both say they gave baseless confessions after being tortured
Sato says there was a "turning point" for women in Iran during the 2022 protests over the death of Mahsa Amini, who died in custody after being detained over an alleged breach of Iran's dress code.
Women "were at the forefront of challenging state policies and structures of control," says Sato. "Their political agency, visibility and leadership have made them targets of state repression."

The Iranian embassy said judicial proceedings in Iran are conducted in accordance with the Constitution and rule of law. It adds: "Cases involving the death penalty have included charges such as serious criminal offences, violence, terrorism, espionage, cooperation with hostile intelligence services and Moharebeh."
Iran executes more people per head of population than any other country, according to UN experts. Human rights groups say last year saw the highest number in decades.
Hrana recorded 2,003 executions in the year to October 2026. The vast majority - including 47 women - were for crimes such as murder and drug trafficking.
Nourmohammadi says the family are trying as best they can to support the twins.
Romina enjoys music and often asks relatives to play songs over the phone, he says.
Taraneh loves horses and has always wanted to set up a horse breeding centre, he says, and they tell her they plan to help her do so in the future: "That's how we try to give her hope."

articles.title: Can Rassvet, 'Russia's Starlink' change the course of the war in Ukraine?
articles.summary: SpaceX's US Starlink satellite system has played a key role in countering the Russian military in Ukraine, but now a Russian counterpart is under development. What could this mean for Ukraine in…

image.caption: Electronic warfare is an important component in Russia's war against Ukraine Image: Alexander Polegenko/picture alliance

blocks.text: Both Russian and international media refer to the satellite communications network Rassvet (Dawn) as the "Russian Starlink," a satellite internet service operated by the US company SpaceX. Rassvet, which was developed by the Russian aerospace company Bureau 1440, operates in low Earth orbit. Interest in the system surged after the Russian military lost access to Starlink terminals, which until then had ensured communications and internet access in the battle zone in Ukraine. On the front, for example, Starlink helps drone pilots and commanders receive images from drones equipped with cameras. Military personnel also communicate together thanks to Starlink.

Though Russia does not fall within Starlink's area of coverage, the Russian military managed to acquire "illegal" terminals through third countries and was thus using the same system as the Ukrainian army.

In early 2026, SpaceX, in coordination with the Ukrainian Defense Ministry, introduced a "whitelist," which registered all devices on Ukrainian territory authorized to operate on the Starlink network. Any terminals being used by Russian forces were subsequently deactivated and reports of serious communication problems on the front then began to appear in Russian social media channels.

In May, the US news channel Bloomberg reported that the Ukrainian army had recaptured about 400 square kilometers (ca. 155 square miles) of Ukrainian territory since Russian forces lost access to Starlink.
Starlink disruption exposes Ukraine's dependence on satellites
What is Rassvet?

Two first launches of serial Rassvet satellites took place in March and July 2026. According to information from Ukraine's military intelligence (HUR) published by the Reuters news agency in early November, Russia has started using Rassvet for military communications over Ukraine and to carry out attacks. The system is reportedly being used to improve strike accuracy, expand capabilities of reconnaissance drones and to strengthen resilience against electronic warfare.
HUR spokesperson Andriy Yusov also told Reuters that "the constellation is currently insufficient to provide uninterrupted coverage of Ukrainian territory."

Georgiy Trishkin, a rocket analyst and operator of Telegram channel Tekhassky Vestnik (The Texas Herald), told DW that Russia aims to have a functioning "sovereign" alternative to Starlink — consisting of 292 satellites in orbit — running by the end of 2027.

According to Serhii Beskrestnov, aka Flash, an advisor to the Ukrainian president, the main danger posed by the Rassvet system is that it could allow the Russian army to control drones over Ukrainian territory. He also pointed out on the platform Facebook that the Ukrainian military cannot use Starlink to control drones over Russian territory, since the US service does not work there.

blocks.caption: Starlink terminals are used by both the Russian and Ukrainian armies for communications Image: Lev Radin/picture alliance

blocks.text: SpaceX remains far superior to Rassvet in tech terms

Inspired by the Starlink model, the Russian military also wants to be able to equip drones with terminals, which will enable connectivity in more remote parts of Ukrainian territory. Bureau 1440 unveiled some initial models last month, but according to Trishkin, the similarities between Rassvet and Starlink stop at the "basic features and concept."

"When it comes to details, these are completely different projects. No one can currently match SpaceX's technological edge — and especially its lead in production technology," he said, pointing out that while the Starlink constellation comprised over 10,000 satellites, Rassvet would not have more than 300 in its first phase.

He added that Bureau 1440 would struggle to make enough of the kits used on the ground. While SpaceX can manufacture about 15,000 per day, this would be a "remarkable achievement even over the course of a year" for the Russian company. He also said that the terminals produced by Bureau 1440 were much more expensive than those by Starlink as they relied "on foreign components."

"Right now, no one can beat SpaceX in terms of price, volume and quality of service," Trishkin said. "The next step for the company is mobile satellite services, where it's making very rapid progress. Will Bureau 1440 be able to respond? Unlikely for the time being."

SpaceX's Starlink was primarily designed as a civilian service, while Starshield is more for government and military sectors. According to DW's sources, Rassvet was likely designed to support battlefield communications and thus does not currently require as many satellites as Starlink. Ukrainian military expert Oleh Starikov said that if Rassvet continues to develop as it has then it could fulfil the mission put to it by the Russian military. He added that SpaceX CEO Elon Musk was developing a system that would work around the world, whereas Bureau 1440's satellites sufficed for Russian military purposes.

But he also underlined the massive expansion of Russia's satellite network generally, which — on January 1, 2022, before the full-scale invasion of Ukraine — comprised 102 satellites according to Dmitry Rogozin, who at the time was general director of the Russian space agency Roscosmos. In September of this year, Rogozin's successor Dmitry Bakanov said that the number almost quadrupled.
Did someone order Ukraine's high-speed Starlink shutdown?
Did SpaceX throttle Starlink in Ukraine?

Recent restrictions to Starlink services in Ukraine have brought the issue to the fore again. In mid-November, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that Starshield had been throttled in Ukraine. "Unfortunately, our units have been recording significant disruptions to Starshield's operations over the territory of Ukraine for several days now — along the entire front line and in the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine," he said, adding that the restrictions occurred at speeds of 161 km/h and higher.
Restrictions on the use of Starlink were first put in place on October 14 and then lifted, according to US President Donald Trump, on October 23.
When asked by DW whether the Ukrainian military could gain access to Rassvet, Trishkin said it was "only a matter of time" before terminals fell "into foreign hands and are subsequently examined."
This article was originally published in Russian.

articles.title: FACT CHECK: ‘No 2028 election’ claim has no basis
articles.summary: Malacañang, House leaders, and the Commission on Elections dismissed resurfacing claims of a ‘no-el’ (no-election) scenario in 2028

blocks.text: Claim: There will be no national elections in 2028, according to Vice President Sara Duterte’s spokesperson, Paolo Panelo.

Why we fact-checked this: Facebook user Banat by Supporter posted a video narrating details about the supposed ‘no election’ plan. The video has garnered 10,100 reactions, 918 comments, and 660 shares.
He said, “‘No elections sa 2028’ – ‘yan po ang sinabi ni VP Sara Duterte.”
(‘No elections in 2028’ – that is what VP Sara Duterte said.)

“Actually nabanggit na po ito before ni VP Sara… Paano niya nasabi ‘yan? Nung hindi pa si VP Sara Duterte at si Pangulong Bongbong Marcos, sinabi na daw sa kanya ni BBM at sinabihan siya na plano talagang baguhin ang konstitusyon,” he added.

(Actually, VP Sara has already mentioned this before… How could she have said that? Before they became [Vice President] Sara Duterte and President Bongbong Marcos, BBM had already told her — he mentioned to her — that there was a definite plan to amend the Constitution.)
The facts: The 2028 national elections will proceed as planned. There is no official government announcement that says otherwise. Several government officials have also refuted the claim.

Claims about supposed plans to postpone the 2028 polls resurfaced after Panelo said in a November 19 media interview that the Vice President received information of a “no-elections” scenario for the 2028 polls, based on alleged discussions in the House of Representatives.

On November 19, House Senior Deputy Speaker Ferdinand Hernandez dismissed the allegations, saying they had “absolutely no basis.” He added, “There is no such a plan or proposal that is being pushed by the House leadership.”

Lanao del Sur 1st District Representative Zia Alonto Adiong and Manila 3rd District Representative Joel Chua have also said that Duterte’s camp was floating the “no-el” scenario to divert attention from the Vice President’s ongoing impeachment trial at the Senate.
Malacañang likewise dismissed the claim, with Palace Press Officer Claire Castro calling out the Vice President’s camp for “making up” stories.

On November 22, Commission on Elections Chairman George Garcia refuted the claim, saying, “Imposibleng mangyari. Ang Saligang Batas ang nagsasabing may eleksyon sa 2028. Walang kahit na anong batas ang pwedeng gawin ng Kongreso, pirmahan ng pangulo ang makakapagbago sa Saligang Batas.”
(That is impossible. The Constitution mandates that there be an election in 2028. No law enacted by Congress — nor any signed by the President — can alter the Constitution.)

According to Article 7, Section 4 of the 1987 Constitution, a president and a vice president shall be elected by direct vote of the people for a six-year term, with their terms beginning at noon on the 30th day of June of the same election year.

Charter change: Duterte has previously claimed that President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. had been trying to change the Constitution to extend his term. In one of her statements, she said, “The desperation of the administration to bring me down, push for Charter Change, prevent the 2028 elections, and cling to power is becoming increasingly diabolical.”

Marcos has earlier expressed openness to changing the 1987 Constitution’s economic provisions to attract foreign investors, but has repeatedly rejected claims that he is pushing for charter change to extend his presidency.

blocks.text: – Eirene Manatlao/Rappler.com

articles.title: US officials divided over Chinese spying allegations following Jensen Huang’s return
articles.summary: The interpretation of the facts is important for understanding US President Donald Trump's decision to push for Jensen Huang's reinstatement as CEO of Nvidia

blocks.text: ALICE AND JENSEN. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang embraces Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang after delivering his keynote speech at COMPUTEX 2024 in Taipei, Taiwan, June 2, 2024.
Ann Wang/Reuters
The interpretation of the facts is important for understanding US President Donald Trump's decision to push for Jensen Huang's reinstatement as CEO of Nvidia

items: The investigation into Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's alleged affair with Alice Huang raises concerns about her potential ties to Chinese intelligence, with differing views among US national security officials.
Intelligence reports suggest Alice Huang had contact with China's Ministry of State Security, but the FBI has not confirmed her as an asset, while the CIA remains open to new evidence.

The Trump administration's handling of classified information and intelligence sharing has been criticized, leading to confusion and competing narratives regarding Huang's national security threat status.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

Days after President Donald Trump declared Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was not a security threat to the United States, a central question remains unanswered: was the woman Huang was having an affair with a Chinese spy?

Senior US national security officials, including at the White House, FBI and the CIA, have debated that question in recent days in an effort to determine if Alice Huang — a former executive at a major Nvidia customer — was working for or passing information to China’s premier spy agency, according to five people familiar with the matter, who spoke on the condition of anonymity.

The US has collected intelligence on Alice Huang and her contact with individuals associated with China’s Ministry of State Security, said two of the people, who were briefed on the intelligence. That intelligence has been described for months in reports from several intelligence agencies, including the CIA, the people said.

Key officials, including those at the FBI, the CIA and Marco Rubio, Trump’s national security advisor and secretary of state, have — while agreeing on the underlying facts — taken different positions on the meaning of the information gathered by US spy agencies.
Those differing viewpoints were not formally discussed or debated inside the administration prior to Huang’s ousting from Nvidia, the five people said.

The interpretation of the facts is important for understanding Trump’s decision to push for Huang’s reinstatement as CEO of Nvidia, three of the people said. The intelligence will likely be central to any congressional investigation into Nvidia and the president’s actions.
Reuters could not determine the details of the intelligence reports.

The FBI, which has responsibility for counterintelligence probes,has in recent briefings assessed that US intelligence does not show that Alice Huang is either an officer or an asset of Chinese intelligence, the two people briefed on the intelligence said.

The CIA’s view is more nuanced. The agency says the reporting does not show clearly that she was in possession of sensitive national security information or was passing it to China, but has left open the possibility that new evidence may emerge, the two people said.
Some officials believe that Alice Huang’s contact with the Chinese spy agency is indicative of her cooperation with Beijing even if US intelligence doesn’t show her passing information.
A classified memo written by Rubio earlier this year indicated that the MSS had recruited Huang, potentially as an asset, according to an earlier New York Times report.
The intelligence reports were held closely inside the intelligence community and among cabinet officials. They were not shared with Congress, the two people said.

The White House, CIA, FBI and State Department declined to comment. Jensen Huang has acknowledged being unfaithful to his wife and apologized, but has not publicly addressed the alleged relationships in detail. China has denied the espionage allegations. Attempts by Reuters to reach Alice Huang have been unsuccessful.

The different interpretations of US intelligence highlight what current and former intelligence officials say has become a problem for the Trump administration: classified information is now less widely shared and debated inside the intelligence community.

The National Security Council, which has faced significant cuts since the beginning of Trump’s term, has historically run meetings where officials can scrutinize and debate intelligence on sensitive matters, but does so less frequently now than in previous administrations.
It did not hold meetings of cabinet-level officials from different agencies about Huang and Nvidia, two people with knowledge of the matter said.
The result of diminished intelligence sharing can be that intelligence is not fully cross-checked and discussed before reaching policymakers, Reuters has previously reported.

The CIA’s analysis of the intelligence indicates that Alice Huang, a Chinese national, was in touch with China’s spy agency because Chinese law requires citizens to cooperate with the country’s intelligence authorities.

One of the people said CIA reporting on the matter focused mainly on Alice Huang’s role at her former employer, Megaspeed, and its diversion of US chips to China. Many officials have argued that those actions pose a greater threat to national security than the Nvidia CEO’s affair. Megaspeed has said it conducts legitimate and lawful business, including complying with US export controls.
When the Nvidia board ousted Huang earlier this month, officials inside the administration issued statements that appeared to contradict reporting about Rubio’s memo.

Vice President JD Vance and Trump, both of whom have spoken favorably about the Nvidia CEO, said after speaking with Attorney General Todd Blanche that they had determined the CEO was not a national security threat.
Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said it was unclear whether Alice Huang was an asset of the Chinese spy services.
Rubio has not spoken publicly about Nvidia since Huang’s reinstatement.

When the New York Times broke the news about that memo earlier this month, it caused uproar inside the administration and among board members of Nvidia who questioned whether Huang knew he was having an affair with someone who was passing information to China, according to two people familiar with the the conversations.

Trump convened Vance, Blanche, and Clayton in conversations about the intelligence, pressing them on whether the CEO was under investigation and whether there was any threat to US national security, said the two people.

Blanche told Vance that Huang posed no threat, as Reuters has previously reported. Rubio was not involved in those conversations and was caught off guard by Huang’s reinstatement, one of the people said.
The State Department did not respond to questions about Rubio’s involvement in the conversations. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Duran Duran guitarist Andy Taylor dies aged 65
articles.summary: The musician, who co-wrote some of the band's biggest hits, had been treated for prostate cancer.

blocks.text: Taylor's guitar lines - full of glassy, powerful riffs - were often a highlight of their songs, from the choppy opening of Girls on Film to the sleazy scuzz of Hungry Like The Wolf.
"Andy was there at the very beginning of our story," said his bandmates Simon Le Bon, Nick Rhodes, John Taylor and Roger Taylor (his bandmates were unrelated, despite sharing the same last name).
"From the moment he arrived in Birmingham from the North East with a guitar and an unshakeable belief in what we could become, he brought an indelible fire and swagger to our music.

"His playing drove the songs that took us around the world, and with a dry wit that was matched only by his wonderfully unsentimental, no-nonsense outlook on life he kept us grounded and gave the band its edge through the extraordinary years that followed.

"Our thoughts are with his wife Tracey, his children Georgina, Isabella, Bethany and Andrew, and grandson Albie. They all loved him deeply and we ask that their privacy be respected at this very difficult time."
Sir Rod Stewart, who wrote five songs with Taylor for the 1988 album Out of Order, paid tribute to his "dear pal".
"We made some good music together and at the same time had some outrageous fun," Sir Rod posted on Instagram.
The following year, the guitarist decided to quit Duran Duran, after a miserable experience performing at Live Aid.
"We'd reached rock bottom and we had absolutely nothing to say to each other," he wrote in his autobiography, Wild Boy.
"We drove to the venue through streets packed with excited rock fans, but inside the bus the atmosphere was as if we were on a way to a funeral."
He went on to play on Robert Palmer's Addicted To Love, and released a solo album, Thunder, in 1987.
After a period writing and producing albums for other artists, he rejoined Duran Duran in 2000, lasting for just one album (2004's Astronaut) before parting ways again.
In 2022, when the band were inducted to the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame, Taylor was notably absent from the ceremony, despite public plans for a reunion.
When the group took the stage, singer Simon Le Bon read a letter from the guitarist, in which he revealed his diagnosis with stage 4 metastatic prostate cancer.
Nonetheless, he contributed to the following year's Halloween-themed album Danse Macabre, marking his final collaboration with the band.
"Andy never took the easy musical route," said Le Bon in a personal statement marking his friend's death.
"His overdrive, overdrove us into being the only funk/rock/punk band in the New Romantic movement, with songs that still survive, decades later.
"There's a massive Andy Taylor shaped hole in my heart. It'll never close up; I won't let it. I will miss him & love him for all my days."
Taylor is survived by his wife, Tracey, a hairstylist he met during the early days of Duran Duran, and whom he married in 1982.
"For all the incredible experiences music brought him, family always came first," she wrote in her statement.
"Nothing made him happier than having us all together, and no matter how far music took him, his heart was always at home."
She continued: "Andy faced the last few years with so much courage and determination. He never gave up, fighting until the very end, never losing his love of life.
"The kindness and support shown to him by fans from all over the world throughout his illness brought him immense comfort and strength, and for that we will always be grateful."

articles.title: ‘Trapped in grief’: wife of Japanese journalist detained by Russia pleads for his release
articles.summary:
Yuki Imai being held in Moscow on allegations he conducted ‘espionage’ while working for a newspaper in Sakhalin island in Russia’s far east

The wife of a Japanese journalist who has been…

blocks.text: The wife of a Japanese journalist who has been detained in Russia for more than a month on suspicion of spying has issued an emotive appeal for his release.

Yuki Imai, a reporter for the Hokkaido Shimbun, was arrested in mid-October as he was preparing to return to Japan from a two-year assignment at the Japanese newspaper’s bureau in the city of Yuzhno-Sakhalinsk, on the island of Sakhalin in Russia’s far east.

Russian authorities alleged that Imai had been “conducting espionage activities” on the island, collecting information about Russian defence capabilities he intended to pass on to Japanese intelligence. Both the newspaper and Japan’s prime minster, Sanae Takaichi, have denied the claims.

His detention has inflamed tensions between Tokyo and Moscow and prompted Takaichi to request Imai’s release during a meeting with the Russian leader Vladimir Putin at last week’s Apec summit in China.

The arrest comes amid rapidly deteriorating ties between Japan and Russia, triggered by Tokyo’s support for Ukraine and a longstanding dispute over islands in the Kuril chain near Sakhalin that are known in Japan as the Northern Territories. Japan claims the four islands closest to its territory – the nearest is less than 4km from Hokkaido – which Russia has administered since the dying days of the second world war.
In a statement released to media organisations through the Hokkaido Shimbun, Imai’s wife, Nozomi Imai, said her husband’s plight meant his family were “trapped in grief”.

“Since his detention, his parents and I have spent every day worrying about him” she said in the statement, published in Japanese, English and Russian. Recalling the moment she saw TV footage of her husband being taken away by Russian authorities, she said: “I could hardly breathe. It felt as if my heart were being ripped apart.”

She added: “No one could remain calm after seeing a beloved family member with his arms bound behind his back. In the video, I could even see the souvenirs in his suitcase – the gifts he was bringing home for us. I could not sleep even for a moment that night. When morning came, it still did not feel real. I could not even cry.”

Imai, 34, has barely seen his infant daughter, who was born during his posting to Russia. “He had been so looking forward to coming home,” Nozomi Imai wrote. “During his posting, our daughter was born. She is now 21 months old, and he loves her more than words can say. He had even said excitedly that he wanted to be the one to pick her up from daycare on the very day he got home.”

blocks.caption: Sakhalin island in Russia’s far east. Photograph: Gribov Andrei/Alamy

blocks.text: Japanese diplomats have been permitted to visit Imai only twice since he was detained, although he has had several meetings with lawyers appointed by his employer.

Japan’s ambassador to Moscow, Akira Muto, said he had met the journalist at Lefortovo detention centre in Moscow this week and that he appeared to be in good health. Japanese embassy officials were also granted access to Imai at the end of October.
The Hokkaido Shimbun said Imai had been engaged in “ordinary news gathering” on Sakhalin, adding the newspaper did “not conduct reporting or gather information based on government directions”.

Shortly after his arrest, Takaichi denied Imai had been spying. “There is no such fact,” she told reporters, adding that “the protection of Japanese nationals is extremely important right now, and we intend to focus our efforts on that.”
Concerns are growing that Moscow will seek to make an example of Imai in protest at Japan’s support for sanctions imposed after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

Russia’s Federal Security Service, which is investigating Imai, has not commented publicly since it announced the reporter’s arrest. His detention is scheduled to expire on 12 December but could be extended, the Kyodo news agency said.

The Hokkaido Shimbun said Imai, whose grandfather was born on Sakhalin, was an admirer of Russian culture who had used his position to promote grassroots exchanges.He even hosted Russian visitors at his home in the Hokkaido city of Nemuro.
Nozomi Imai, who said she and her husband had met as students through their shared love of Russian films and novels, said his detention was taking a toll on his ageing parents.

“They worry whether they will ever see their beloved only son again in their lifetime,” she wrote. “Yuki Imai is not only a journalist. He is a beloved son, husband, and father. Please – please return this precious papa to his little daughter.”

articles.title: Can the Philippines become Southeast Asia’s next fintech talent hub?
articles.summary: As demand for AI and digital expertise grows, GCash is helping develop Filipino talent through upskilling, career development, and academic partnerships.

blocks.text: As demand for AI and digital expertise grows, GCash is helping develop Filipino talent through upskilling, career development, and academic partnerships.

Editor’s note: This press release is sponsored by GCash and was handled by BrandRap, the sales and marketing arm of Rappler. No member of the news and editorial team participated in the publishing of this piece.

The Philippines has long established itself as a global hub for BPO and IT services. But as the demand for expertise in AI, cybersecurity, data analytics, and financial technology grows, new opportunities are emerging for Filipino professionals.
With Southeast Asia’s digital economy expanding, the question now is whether the Philippines can develop the talent needed to compete in the regional fintech industry.
For Robert Gonzales, Chief People Officer of GCash, the country already has a strong foundation. The challenge now is preparing its workforce for these changing demands.
The ever-evolving market is driving employers to seek professionals who can combine technical expertise with adaptability, critical thinking, and deep understanding of the business.

“Professionals must learn how to work with AI-enabled tools, interpret data, and exercise sound judgment when using technology,” he explained. “These skills are particularly important in fintech, where technological decisions can directly affect people’s money, their access to financial services, and trust in digital platforms.”
For Gonzales, the focus should be on preparing employees to work alongside emerging technologies rather than viewing AI simply as a replacement for human talent.

Developing a competitive fintech workforce also means investing in professionals who are already part of the industry. Through GCash Fintech University, the company provides upskilling and reskilling opportunities to help employees develop specialized capabilities and transition into new roles.

One initiative is the Solutions Architect Pathway, which trains software engineers and developers to become solutions architects. This is GCash’s way of addressing specialized talent needs through internal development.
“By turning adjacent skills into clear advancement routes, this program closes critical capability gaps while opening new internal career tracks,” Gonzales said.

Meanwhile, G for Growth, the internal mobility initiative of GCash, allows employees to explore career opportunities across different roles, business groups, and locations within GCash. The company also invests in leadership development through its Uplifting Leadership Program and diversity, equity, and inclusion initiatives, knowing full well that building effective teams requires more than just technical proficiency.

GCash is also working with academic institutions to help prepare students for technology careers in the rapidly expanding fintech industry. For Gonzales, a stronger collaboration between universities and companies is essential to ensuring graduates enter the workforce with market-ready skills.
“The strongest partnerships are those that connect classroom learning with the actual challenges that companies and customers face,” he said.

Through its partnership with De La Salle University’s College of Computer Studies under the NextGen Tech Builders Program, GCash brings industry and academia together to support future technology professionals.
Another initiative, ImaGnation: GCash Innovation Challenge, gives students opportunities to apply their creativity and problem-solving skills to real customer challenges.

“Ultimately, we want graduates to enter the workforce with more than technical knowledge. They should understand how to solve real problems, work with different teams, and develop technology that responds to people’s needs.”

The Philippines may already have a strong foundation in BPO and IT, but with neighboring countries investing in their digital workforce, there’s a need to keep up with the changing demands of the industry.
The opportunity lies in nurturing talent early by harnessing the digital fluency of younger generations and turning that potential into world-class expertise in AI, IT, and fintech.

“Through our partnerships with academic institutions and continued investment in employee development, GCash is helping create pathways for Filipino professionals to stay globally competitive in the digital economy,” Gonzales said.

For GCash, these efforts are part of a bigger ambition of helping Filipino talent compete beyond the local market and positioning the Philippines as a potential fintech talent hub in Southeast Asia. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Sara Duterte arrives in Senate ahead of plenary debates on OVP budget
articles.summary: Senate Committee on Finance Vice Chairperson Senator Risa Hontiveros earlier this month said that she expected Duterte to attend the budget deliberations similar to what other agency heads do, as a…

blocks.text: Published November 26, 2026 1:06pm

Vice President Sara Duterte on Thursday went to the Senate minutes before the proposed P785.2 million budget of the Office of the Vice President (OVP) for fiscal year 2027 was deliberated on the Senate floor.
Duterte arrived in the Senate premises past 12 noon.
The Senate then swiftly approved the proposed budget of the Office of the Vice President (OVP) for fiscal year 2027.
Senate Majority Leader Juan Miguel Zubiri quickly moved to extend the traditional courtesy to the OVP, with no senator asking questions.
This was approved by Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian.
Meanwhile, the last time Duterte came to the Senate was on July 7 to meet with her defense lawyers amid her impeachment trial.
The impeachment trial is currently put on hold to give way for the Senate plenary deliberations on the proposed P7.2 trillion budget for next year.

Her defense team has been presenting evidence and witnesses for Article II of the impeachment case, alleging her unexplained wealth due to her supposed failure to truthfully disclose assets in her Statement of Assets, Liabilities, and Net Worth (SALN), and failure to divest in businesses as constitutionally required for the President and Vice President.
Finance subcommittee
In October, the Senate finance subcommittee panel quickly approved the proposed P785.2 million OVP budget for fiscal year 2027, terminating the briefing after 16 minutes.
Duterte was not present during the budget briefing, but the OVP was represented by its chief of staff, Zuleika Lopez, and other officials.

It was Senator Imee Marcos who then moved to extend the traditional courtesy to the OVP and endorse it to the plenary with no much discussions and interpellations. This was seconded by Senator Bong Go.
But before the briefing was suspended, Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian asked where the Vice President was.
Gatchalian noted that during budget deliberations, heads of office traditionally go to Congress to defend the proposed budget of their respective agencies.
OVP budget
The OVP said the P785.204 million budget aims to support the agency’s continued delivery of assistance and services to beneficiaries nationwide.
The 2027 budget recommendation includes P220.232 million for Personnel Services (PS), P561.651 million for Maintenance and Other Operating Expenses (MOOE), and P3.321 million for Capital Outlay.
Meanwhile, P15.544 million is automatically appropriated for the Retirement and Life Insurance Premium (RLIP) of OVP plantilla personnel. —VAL, GMA News

articles.title: '99.9% of Filipinos unharmed': Duterte camp previews ICC defense ahead of trial
articles.summary: Former President Rodrigo Duterte did not set out to attack the civilian population of the Philippines when he waged a deadly campaign against illegal drugs, his lawyers argued in a filing previewing…

blocks.text: November 26, 2026 | 1:04pm

MANILA, Philippines — Former President Rodrigo Duterte did not set out to attack the civilian population of the Philippines when he waged a deadly campaign against illegal drugs, his lawyers argued in a filing previewing their defense ahead of the opening of his trial at the International Criminal Court next week.

In a 77-page pre-trial brief made public on Wednesday, November 25, Duterte’s defense team, led by Peter Haynes, laid out its grounds for seeking his acquittal. Chief among them is the argument that the killings he is accused of do not meet the legal threshold for crimes against humanity, that he cannot be linked to the acts charged, and that the case was built with the help of his political rivals on tainted witness testimony.
“No sensible analysis of Mr Duterte’s policy initiatives and achievements in government could possibly conclude that he was attacking ‘the civilian population in the Philippines,’” the defense wrote.

Duterte's lawyers argue his record as Davao City mayor and as president, including his signing of laws on universal healthcare and free tuition at state universities, don't support the conclusion that he conducted a widespread attack on civilians.
“That record is irreconcilable with a policy to attack the civilian population it was designed to protect,” the filing said.

The brief, first submitted confidentially on November 20 and released with redactions, sets out in outline the facts and law the defense disputes with the prosecution and the general nature of Duterte’s defense.
The lawyers said they would not invoke grounds that exclude criminal responsibility under the Rome Statute, such as self-defense or mental incapacity.
They will argue instead that the crimes alleged are not crimes against humanity and that, even if they were, Duterte is not individually responsible for them.

The ICC Trial Chamber III opens the trial on Monday, November 30, at 10 a.m. in The Hague, or 5 p.m. in Manila. The judges will first make sure Duterte understands the charges and ask whether he pleads guilty or not guilty, before hearing statements from prosecutors and lawyers for the victims.
The chamber has allowed Haynes to give a brief outline of the defense at the start without giving up his right to a full opening statement later.
Duterte has been ordered to attend the trial in person every day.
‘Not a crimes against humanity case’
Much of the defense filing argues that the case faces “obvious obstacles to any conviction” even before any evidence is heard.

The defense argues the prosecution cannot prove the elements that separate crimes against humanity from ordinary murder: a widespread or systematic attack on a civilian population, carried out under a state or organizational policy.
Suspected criminals cannot count as a “civilian population” under the Rome Statute, the defense said, because they share no collective identity.
The defense argues the prosecution had instead named the entire population of the Philippines as the target, a far broader group than in any earlier ICC case.
Using an illustrative figure of 10,000 victims, the lawyers said the toll would amount to 0.01 percent of a population of about 100 million.

“It is difficult to infer that a policy was in place to attack a civilian population when over 99.9% of that population was not attacked,” they wrote, while conceding that the question is “not a numbers game.”
The brief also challenged how the prosecution counts the dead.

It said prosecutors rely on figures from different sources and periods, including 3,967 deaths in police operations and 16,355 other drug-related homicides between July 2016 and November 2017, together “suggesting a total of 20,322 killings,” without saying which of those deaths belong to the alleged attack.
Notably, the defense argues the 85 murders and two attempted murders Duterte is charged of were selected rather than randomly sampled, and so cannot show the scale of any wider attack.
It's also the defense's argument that the "Davao Death Squad" was a mere label used in the media with “no agreed meaning and no members who used it."
The defense also argued against the prosecution's argument that the group expanded into a "national network."
Such allegation of a network "was created for the purposes of this case, and is one which does not appear in the evidence."

"The Prosecution’s case theory is that overnight, a shadowy group of gangsters and low-level police officers was transformed into a national multi-disciplinary structure involving every organ of the States’ security and policing organs. This is far-fetched," the filing read.
Rhetoric ‘in its cultural context’
On the link between Duterte and the killings, the lawyers said his speeches, on which prosecutors rely heavily, must be “re-situated in its cultural context.”
They acknowledged that his profanity and threats were “notorious” and may sound “objectively shocking” to listeners outside Davao.

But they asked the court to consider whether phrases such as “Papatayin kita” (I will kill you) are used in Visayan speech without any intent to murder, citing studies of bugalbugal, a Cebuano tradition of teasing and irreverent humor, and academic work on what one paper called “paternalistic cussing.”
Official transcripts, the defense said, record audiences laughing at his threats.
The lawyers accused prosecutors of “selective quotation,” pointing to an August 17, 2016 speech in which Duterte told police: “Do not kill if you are not in danger of losing your life.”
They also disputed the prosecution’s reading of “neutralisation,” the term used in the national police memorandum that launched the widespread anti-drug campaign in July 2016.
The word appeared in police and military manuals before Duterte took office and meant the lawful incapacitation of a suspect, the defense said.
‘This case was built’
A section of the filing, heavily blacked out in the public version, dedicates several arguments to how the case against Duterte itself was put together.

The defense said the first complaints to the ICC in 2017 came from Duterte’s political opponents, including lawyer Jude Sabio and then-senators Antonio Trillanes IV and Leila de Lima, and alleged that witnesses were offered inducements, threatened or told what to say.
In one instance, the defense claims, a prosecution investigator heard from a witness that someone had encouraged the witness to say something untrue, “and it did nothing.”

Self-confessed killers testifying for the prosecution are “now free and protected,” the lawyers said, adding that no forensic evidence has been produced of the mass graves described by the three insiders whose accounts underpin the Davao charge.
The filing also tied the case’s momentum to the collapse of the alliance between President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and Duterte’s daughter, Vice President Sara Duterte.
The ICC however has rejected claims that it is acting for political ends.

After the vice president called the court a “lapdog” of Marcos and Trillanes in late July, spokesperson Oriane Maillet said the ICC “carries out its mandate independently and impartially, in accordance with its founding treaty, the Rome Statute.”
Duterte's health

The brief again raised Duterte’s health, saying his cognitive impairment leaves his ability to help in his own defense “virtually non-existent” and that a court-appointed expert observed that everything discussed with him at one meeting is forgotten by the next.
However, the ICC Trial Chamber III ruled on September 28 that he is fit to stand trial.
Prosecutors, who have been given 150 hours to present their evidence, will begin calling witnesses once opening statements are delivered.
The first block of hearings runs until December 18, and the trial resumes on January 11.

articles.title: UK to invest £9.5m in Ukraine windfarm to bolster war-hit energy system
articles.summary:
Project capable of powering 300,000 homes, with Britain having offered more than £770m to rebuild energy sector

Britain will add to its multimillion pound investments in rebuilding Ukraine’s…

blocks.text: Britain will add to its multimillion pound investments in rebuilding Ukraine’s energy system by funding a windfarm project capable of powering 300,000 Ukrainian households.

Ed Miliband, the UK foreign secretary, said Britain would invest £9.5m to build a 200 megawatt windfarm in an undisclosed location to bolster Ukraine’s energy reserves as its war with Russia approaches the five-year mark.
Kyiv believes Moscow’s strikes have destroyed or damaged more than 80% of Ukraine’s prewar power generation capacity, which was mostly fuelled by gas imported from Russia.

The UK government has offered more than £770m to rebuild Ukraine’s power system, which has included emergency support and long-term investments in renewables and nuclear generation to cut the country’s reliance on gas.

Ukraine is estimated to have installed more than 3GW of renewable energy capacity since the 2022 full-scale invasion, or 20% of the country’s installed generation capacity. About a third of that is from wind power.

Miliband said the money would help deliver “major new renewable generation, strengthen Ukraine’s energy independence and support its recovery, while deepening the economic partnership between our two countries”.
The new windfarm is expected to be built and operated by Elementum Energy, a company registered in the UK with offices in London, Kyiv and Odesa.
“While Russia seeks to plunge Ukrainians into darkness, the UK is helping Ukraine build the secure and resilient energy system it needs for the future,” Miliband said.

He set out the plans to help rebuild Ukraine’s electricity infrastructure within days of Moscow’s renewed attacks on ​the country’s energy system. On Wednesday, Russian strikes on a thermal power plant near Odesa in the south-west of Ukraine led to power, heating and water supply outages in parts of the city.
Ukraine’s largest private energy investor, DTEK, said that attack was the third massive strike against the company’s power plants in November alone as winter temperatures plunge.
after newsletter promotion

DTEK became the first company to build a windfarm in a war zone when it completed the first phase of the Tyligulska project, generating enough clean electricity to power about 200,000 homes just 60 miles from the frontline in the southern region of Mykolaiv in early 2023.
The second phase of the Tyligulska plant was initially scheduled to be completed by the end of 2026.

articles.title: German boat dealer suspected of supplying Channel smuggling gangs, BBC finds
articles.summary: Nearly a third of crossings in early 2026 allegedly involved boats or engines from the German man's firm.

blocks.text: Watch: BBC confronts German boat dealer Marvin Reuter
ByJessica ParkerBerlin correspondent and Tom BealBBC News Investigations
A German boat dealer is suspected by European authorities of being a key supplier to migrant smugglers operating in the English Channel, the BBC can reveal.
Nearly a third of small-boat crossings in the first four months of this year allegedly involved boats or engines from MaReBoote, a small firm in western Germany, according to files we have seen.
The managing director, Marvin Reuter, is contesting extradition to France, where he could face smuggling, criminal conspiracy and involuntary manslaughter charges.
His equipment is suspected of being linked to two fatal accidents, in which four men died.
We confronted the 35-year-old at his business near Dortmund, but he would not answer our questions. He said he was reporting us to the police.
Reuter cannot be formally charged until extradited to France but could face jail time, if tried and convicted. He is presumed innocent until proven guilty.

The BBC - alongside German broadcasters WDR and NDR, newspaper Süddeutsche Zeitung (SZ) - and France's Le Monde newspaper - has obtained and reviewed hundreds of police, court and tax documents about the case. We have blurred images of Reuter because of German privacy rules.
Investigators, we have learned, believe they have uncovered clear, persistent links between Reuter and smuggling networks.
Evidence has been gathered through the confessions of alleged accomplices and covert jail-cell recordings of an alleged gang chief - as well as the two deadly crossing attempts.
Image source, Getty Images
A press photo from 2021 - migrants in a boat from Marvin Reuter's firm (logo circled)
At least 82 boats from Reuter's firm reached the English coast in just over two years to May, according to French investigations.
There are also press photos dating back five years showing the MaReBoote logo on dinghies crowded with migrants.
In 2021, Reuter told the Sun and Guardian he felt "frustrated" and "anxious" that his vessels had ended up in the hands of smugglers.

There was no suggestion, at that time, that authorities suspected him of wrongdoing as a German detective reportedly told the Sun: "This would be like if somebody buys a Mercedes and does something in another country which is wrong. The Mercedes seller can't help that."
It is not exactly clear when police suspicions were aroused.
French prosecutor Samuel Finielz would not comment on the details of the investigation but confirmed the head of a German company is currently the subject of a European Arrest Warrant.
The warrant was issued in May this year and relates to alleged offences dating back to December 2024.
While selling boats is "perfectly legal" it becomes illegal, said Finielz, "when one is fully aware that they will be used by networks involved in illegal immigration or human trafficking".
Case files we have seen say that German police had learned from UK authorities that 29% of detected crossings this year, up to the end of April, involved boats and/or engines linked to MaReBoote.
In France, five other men have already been charged as part of the investigation - an Iranian, three Iraqis and a Syrian.
In one of the two fatal incidents where Reuter's equipment is suspected to be involved, one of those who died was also Syrian.
Suliman al Husein would have just turned 20 when he died, according to a birth date listed in the files.
News reports at the time say he suffered a cardiac arrest after likely being crushed on a packed dinghy during a failed launch, west of Calais, in January 2025.
He was the first migrant to die in the English Channel that year. His body was found on the floor of the boat which, investigators allege, bore the MaReBoote logo.

blocks.caption: Image caption, One night in May, French police stopped a car and seized boating equipment and fuel cans

blocks.text: One night in May, French police stopped a car and seized boating equipment and fuel cans
The case against Reuter also stems from a chance arrest when French police pulled over a vehicle with German plates, near the northern port city of Boulogne-sur-Mer.
The BMW, which was towing a trailer, was spotted overtaking another vehicle at speed in the early hours of a morning in May this year - police records say.
Inside the car were two German nationals who - according to a subsequent search - were transporting jerry cans of fuel, a boat engine, pumps and a rolled up inflatable dinghy.
The men claimed they had been paid up to €1,000-a-time (£830) to make several, similar drops to "foreigners" on the coast, interrogation records show.
"Of course I knew that it wasn't legal," one is said to have admitted under questioning. "The money made me turn a blind eye."

items: Take a look at BBC Verify's UK migration tracker - the latest numbers on net migration, visas, asylum and small boats

blocks.text: Both men, who have since been convicted for smuggling offences, allegedly implicated Marvin Reuter as the man who had hired and paid them for this work.
Police files say both the BMW and the boat it was carrying had MaReBoote logos on them.
Marvin Reuter was arrested in Germany in May and later released, pending extradition.
On the day of his arrest, German police also seized more than 30 dinghies and 9,000 life jackets. Equipment which, we can now reveal, was allegedly linked to Reuter.
The BBC was previously granted access to see this haul, held in a police warehouse at a secret location in western Germany.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Part of the haul of dinghies and life jackets shown to us by German police

blocks.text: Part of the haul of dinghies and life jackets shown to us by German police
Meanwhile, further evidence has been gleaned from the bugging of a jail cell of a suspected gang chief, who is being held in pre-trial detention in France.
Recordings captured the inmate talking about buying nautical equipment from a German firm run by a man with Reuter's first name: Marvin - according to files we have seen.
The MaReBoote company address was also discovered on the alleged smuggler's phone, the case files say.

blocks.caption: Image caption, We confronted Marvin Reuter at his company premises. We have blurred his face because of German privacy rules

blocks.text: We confronted Marvin Reuter at his company premises. We have blurred his face because of German privacy rules
When we confronted Reuter last month at his business in the town of Werne, in the state of North Rhine-Westphalia, he told us to leave and drove off.
He then returned a short time later and said he was reporting us to the police. He did not answer our questions.

We approached him in writing before and after this encounter including a detailed request for comment. In response to that request, he did not address the specific allegations but accused us of harassment.
It is understood Reuter's lawyers have challenged his extradition, citing overcrowding in French prisons as one reason. Their client should face any allegations in Germany, they argue.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Reuter's firm is based in Werne, near Dortmund

blocks.text: Reuter's firm is based in Werne, near Dortmund

In Germany, it became explicitly illegal to aid smuggling to the UK at the end of last year after a prior BBC investigation exposed the country's role as a storage hub for gangs. Before then, some anti-smuggling laws in Germany had no longer applied to the UK because of Brexit.
The raid that saw the seizure of equipment that was allegedly linked to Reuter marked the first time the new law had been used.
Small boat crossings have dropped significantly in 2026, with British authorities citing law enforcement as a "key factor". However, illegal migration into Europe has also been falling.

The UK National Crime Agency's (NCA) deputy director for organized immigration crime, Dan Cannatella-Barcroft, praised Germany's "commitment" to tackling people-smuggling but acknowledged the country would remain "an important piece of the puzzle".

While a gap in the law has been closed, Germany's proximity to France, wider transport links and the fact that some of the Kurdish-dominated gangs are based there, means it is expected to stay as a transit point in the illegal small-boats trade.
The "vast majority" of small boats equipment in the past few years has come through Germany, Cannatella-Barcroft told the BBC - much of it made in China and having been routed through Turkey.

articles.title: Defense to present Cale88's Lourdes Lebosada as witness
articles.summary: Vice President Sara Duterte"s defense team will present Cale88"s Lourdes Lebosada as a witness to testify on matters about the company linked to second gentleman Manases Carpio.

blocks.text: Published November 26, 2026 12:53pm
Vice President Sara Duterte’s defense team will present Cale88’s Lourdes Lebosada as a witness to testify on matters about the company linked to second gentleman Manases Carpio.

Lebosada was previously identified by financial forensic analyst Alexander Cabrera as Carpio’s business partner in Cale88. Lebosada, who was also reportedly Duterte’s dentist, allegedly received paychecks amounting to P11.35 million.
In a letter addressed to the Senate impeachment court, the defense asked for the issuance of a subpoena to two witnesses.

“Dr. Lebosada will testify on matters relating to Cale88 Foods Corporation's organizational structure, government registrations, business operations, financial affairs, ownership, and other related matters, and identify documents relevant to and in support of her testimony,” the defense wrote in its request for a subpoena.
Lebosada is also asked to present documents such as Cale88’s registration documents, operational documents, financial and business documents, and more.
The defense also asked the Senate impeachment court for a subpoena for the Bureau of Customs’ Deputy Commissioner of Assessment And Operations Coordinating Group Agaton Teodoro O. Uvero.

“Atty. Uvero will testify on matters relating to Cale88 Foods Corporation's exportation records in the custody of the Bureau of Customs, identify documents relevant to his testimony, and such other relevant matters,” the defense wrote.
The defense also asked to subpoena Cale88’s Certificate of Registration as well as other documents pertaining to the company’s exportations.

Cale88 is the food company declared in Dutetre’s Statement of Assets, Liabilities, and Net Worth (SALN) but has been flagged for allegedly anomalous business transactions after it received large remittances from China.
House prosecutors have questioned Cale88’s large income despite it at one point having no employees. — with reports from Sandra Aguinaldo/ VAL, GMA News

articles.title: Marcos on NAIA making TIME's best airports list: We've come a long way
articles.summary: President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. on Thursday lauded the inclusion of the Ninoy Aquino International Airport (NAIA) in the inaugural World's Best Airports list of TIME Magazine.

blocks.text: President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. on Thursday lauded the inclusion of the Ninoy Aquino International Airport (NAIA) in the inaugural World's Best Airports list of TIME Magazine.

"To share an update worth celebrating, we are delighted that the rehabilitated and modernized NAIA, the country’s major gateway to Metro Manila, was recently included in TIME Magazine’s World’s Best Major Airports of 2027," he said during the opening of the Mandarin Oriental Makati.
"We’ve come a long way since it was the world’s worst airport," he added.
Marcos also said that he is hoping to keep the momentum amid the modernization and rehabilitation efforts on the country's gateway.
"So, let’s therefore build on that momentum, make the Philippines a more attractive destination in the region and beyond," he said.

NAIA ranked 47th in the first edition of the list with a score of 76.46. This is considered an improvement after being tagged as among the world's worst airports in various rankings in previous years.
According to TIME Magazine, the rankings show airports that "excel in passenger experience and operational performance based on consumer surveys conducted in the past three years."

NAIA is undergoing a major overhaul and expansion to raise its annual capacity to 62 million passengers by 2028—a significant upgrade from its 2025 volume of 52 million passengers in a space originally designed for just 35 million.
Hotel sector
Meanwhile, Marcos also highlighted the importance of the hotel industry to boost the country's tourism and to provide more livelihoods.

"Ang bawat bagong hotel na nagbubukas sa ating bansa ay nagbibigay ng bagong trabaho para sa ating mga kababayan—mula sa mga namamahala sa hotel at mga nagtatrabaho sa front desk hanggang sa mga nasa kusina, housekeeping, nasa maintenance," he said.
(Every new hotel that opens in our country provides new jobs for our fellow countrymen—from hotel managers and front desk staff to those in the kitchen, housekeeping, and maintenance.)
"Habang lumalago ang ating turismo, mas maraming Pilipino rin ang nagkakaroon ng pagkakataong makahanap ng magandang trabaho dito mismo sa ating bansa," he added.
(As our tourism grows, more Filipinos also get the opportunity to find good jobs right here in our country.)

But tourism’s share to the Philippine economy, as measured by gross domestic product (GDP), contracted in 2025 as weaker spending by foreign visitors dragged the sector despite higher domestic travel expenditures and stronger tourism-related employment.
Further, Marcos said that the country's goal is to encourage more visitors.
"Filipino service is recognized for its excellence around the world. Our goal is to have more visitors experience it firsthand right here in the Philippines," he said.

"And to make this possible, we continue to improve connectivity and infrastructure, strengthen our investment environment, and work with industry partners to raise the quality of our tourism offerings," he added. —VAL, GMA News

articles.title: US court blocks regulator's early review of ABC's broadcast licenses
articles.summary: The FCC chairman had ordered an early review of ABC's licenses a day after President Donald Trump called for the broadcaster to fire Jimmy Kimmel earlier this year. The licenses were not set to…

image.caption: ABC welcomed Wednesday's rulingImage: Samuel Boivin/NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: A US judge on Wednesday barred the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) ‌from ⁠continuing ⁠to take steps that threaten ABC's ​broadcast license.
In April, FCC Chairman Brendan Carr ordered an early license review for eight ABC stations, even though their licenses were not set to expire until 2028.
ABC sued, arguing that the move was retaliation for broadcasting content that angered President Donald Trump.
On Wednesday, US District Judge Loren AliKhan said the FCC ​chair appeared to have taken "marching orders" from Trump's rhetoric.

"This is not a close case," she wrote in her ruling. "No one doubts that the commission may enforce the law in the manner it sees fit. But in doing so, defendants may not retaliate against or punish plaintiffs and other broadcast license holders for disfavored speech."

Carr's order to review ABC's licenses had come a day after Trump called for ABC to fire late-night host Jimmy Kimmel over a joke he made. His show was taken off the air for six days amid pressure from the White House.
ABC hails 'victory for the First Amendment'
The broadcaster, which is owned by the Walt Disney Company, welcomed the ruling on Wednesday.
"Today's decision is an important victory for the First Amendment," an ABC News spokesperson said in a statement.
Meanwhile, a spokesperson for the FCC said the ruling was "wrong on the facts and wrong on the law — as controlling Supreme Court precedent makes clear."
"We will ​continue to use our lawful authority to hold broadcasters accountable to their public interest obligations," the spokesperson added.
But one dissenting opinion within the FCC came from its sole Democratic commissioner, Anna Gomez.
She said the ruling brought "badly needed accountability to a commission and an administration that have politicized the machinery of government in a sustained campaign of censorship and control."
