articles.title: Rodrigo Duterte at ICC: A cheat sheet on understanding his case, trial
articles.summary: Find answers to questions like: who are his co-perpetrators, what will happen during the trial, and can the decision be appealed?

blocks.text: DUTERTE. Former president Rodrigo Duterte appears before the International Criminal Court, as the court hears arguments regarding Duterte's health and ability to stand trial, while he faces murder charges related to his war on drugs, in The Hague, Netherlands, on September 16 2026.
Piroschka van de Wouw/Pool via Reuters
Find answers to questions like: who are his co-perpetrators, what will happen during the trial, and can the decision be appealed?

items: Former Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte will be tried at the International Criminal Court for crimes against humanity related to his war on drugs, marking him as the first Filipino and Asian leader to face such charges.
Duterte is facing three counts of murder and attempted murder, with allegations stemming from his tenure as Davao City mayor and president

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

On Monday, November 30, former president Rodrigo Duterte, 81, will become the first Filipino and Asian head of state to be tried over a crimes-against-humanity case at the International Criminal Court (ICC) in The Hague, Netherlands.
He was arrested by Philippine authorities in March 2025 and was turned over the tribunal’s jurisdiction immediately. Duterte has been detained at the Scheveningen Prison since then.
The former president will be on trial because in April, the ICC Pre-Trial Chamber I confirmed all three charges against him.
Here’s a cheat sheet to easily understand Duterte’s case and his upcoming trial.
Duterte is facing a three counts of crimes against humanity case of murder and attempted murder.

This is because of his war on drugs launched in 2016, and the killings of the Davao Death Squad. The case’s coverage is from November 1, 2011, to March 16, 2019 — years that the Philippines was part of the court and when Duterte served as Davao City mayor and Philippine president.
The counts are divided into these alleged crimes:

items: 1st count: Murder in Davao City when Duterte was mayor
2nd count: Murder of high-value targets
3rd count: Murder and attempted murder during barangay-level drug war operations

blocks.caption: Inside story: Rodrigo Duterte’s ICC arrest

blocks.text: In February, the prosecution named eight persons tagged as Duterte’s indirect co-perpetrators. They were former officials who have alleged direct and indirect participation in implementing the drug war that killed nearly 30,000, according to several human rights groups.
They are:

items: Senator Ronald “Bato” dela Rosa
Former police chief Vicente Danao
The late former police chief Camilo Cascolan
Former police chief Oscar Albayalde
Senator Bong Go
Former National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) chief Dante Gierran
Former Philippine Drug Enforcement Agency chief Isidro Lapeña
Former justice secretary Vitaliano Aguirre II

blocks.text: Dela Rosa has a standing warrant of arrest, but remains at-large as of writing.

blocks.caption: ICC warrant details Bato dela Rosa’s role in drug war

blocks.text: November 30 is the start of the actual trial.

The hearing will open with Duterte being asked if he understands the nature of his cases. He will likewise be asked to enter a plea — guilty or not guilty. This is similar to an arraignment in local cases.
Afterwards, the prosecution and the common legal representatives of the victims (CLRVs) will have their opening statements.
It will be up to the defense if they will deliver an opening statement too. The prosecution will then present their witnesses after the opening statements. This is expected to run for several months.

After the prosecution’s presentation, CLRVs won’t present evidence but rather submit observations. As in a regular trial, the defense will have the opportunity to present their case and evidence too, to rebut the prosecution’s allegations.

These hearings could last for years, depending on the pace. In the end, the judges will decide to either acquit or convict Duterte. A conviction will demand from the prosecution presenting evidence that is beyond reasonable doubt.

blocks.caption: Here’s what to expect at the opening of Rodrigo Duterte’s ICC trial

blocks.text: In the Philippines, only conviction is appealable. Some parties use other remedies, like a certiorari, in cases of acquittal. Certiorari is essentially an order to a lower court to present case records for review by a higher court.

But in the ICC, both the prosecution and the defense may appeal the judgment before the ICC appeals chamber. This means that either way, the judgment against Duterte may be brought to a higher chamber after the promulgation.
Like in other cases, the ICC may impose prison time, a fine, or even forfeiture of property or assets.
The maximum jail time could be up to 30 years, but the ICC imposes life imprisonment in extreme cases. It has no death penalty.
The Scheveningen Prison is designed only for short-term detention. Once convicted, the ICC said Duterte will be transferred to a prison of a state designated by the Court.
This state will be determined based on the list of nations that are willing to accept convicted persons.
Duterte had repeatedly questioned the ICC’s jurisdiction over his case. Jurisdiction determines whether the court is the proper avenue and has the power to try his case.

blocks.caption: EXPLAINER: What you need to know about ICC’s jurisdiction over Duterte

blocks.text: With finality, the ICC appeals chamber denied Duterte’s challenge in April and cleared the way for the November 30 trial. This jurisdiction challenge was among the options left for Duterte to derail his ICC proceedings.
Had Duterte won the challenge, it would have stopped his case and he may have been able to return home. But he lost, so he will remain detained for the duration of his trial. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Kim Jong Un tours nuclear material sites, urges wider use of tactical nuclear weapons
articles.summary: North Korea's Kim Jong Un visited sites that produce nuclear material and told his military to focus on tactical weapons, saying his country's nuclear status is irreversible.

image.caption: Images released by the state media showed Kim walking through rows of what appeared to be uranium-enrichment centrifugesImage: KCNA/REUTERS

blocks.text: North Korean leader Kim Jong Un toured factories that make nuclear material, along with a research institute, and pressed for the wider use of tactical nuclear weapons, state media reported on Thursday.

The visit took place on Wednesday, but the state news agency KCNA did not provide the location of the sites. Photos showed Kim walking between rows of what appeared to be centrifuges for enriching uranium. Analysts also spotted small, standardized tactical warheads such as the Hwasan-31.
What did Kim say?

Kim said North Korea's production capacity for nuclear material is being steadily expanded. He said tactical weapons should be used in different areas and for different missions, citing the danger from a hostile state on his border, referring to neighbor South Korea.
He also accused the United States of encouraging its allies to seek nuclear-powered submarines and to share nuclear weapons.

"Our possession of nuclear weapons is an absolutely irreversible choice as long as malicious forces exist that use nuclear weapons as a means of achieving hegemony," Kim said, adding that he would treat any attempt to deny North Korea's nuclear status, which was written into its constitution in 2023, as a declaration of war.
Kim said Pyongyang would not seek approval from other countries.
What does it mean for dialogue?
Lim Eul-chul, a professor at South Korea's Kyungnam University, said the visit signals Kim's desire to change the circumstances of any future talks on North Korea's weapons programs.

"This is not so much North Korea permanently closing the door to dialogue with the United States as a strategy of raising the bar: 'denuclearisation talks' are over, and if talks open in future, it will deal only on a 'nuclear state versus nuclear state' basis," he told Reuters news agency.

South Korean news agency Yonhap said this was Kim's fourth visit to a nuclear facility since September 2024. It came about a week after US President Donald Trumpvisited China for the APEC summit, where Kim did not publicly respond to an offer to meet.

articles.title: Ombudsman upholds graft raps vs ex-Bohol mayor over Christmas tree billboard
articles.summary: The Office of the Ombudsman has affirmed its indictment of former Guindulman, Bohol Mayor Albino Balo, five former and current municipal officials and a private contractor for graft, following…

blocks.text: November 26, 2026 | 12:10pm
Philstar.com / File

MANILA, Philippines — The Office of the Ombudsman has affirmed its indictment of former Guindulman, Bohol Mayor Albino Balo, five former and current municipal officials and a private contractor for graft, following allegations that a giant Christmas tree was unlawfully passed off as a newly procured, government-funded billboard.

In separate orders issued on November 25, the Ombudsman also upheld the administrative dismissal from service of Balo and the five local government employees, affirming its earlier finding of Grave Misconduct.
The administrative ruling affirms a 2025 Ombudsman decision imposing dismissal from service on Balo, Labang, Janiola, Beronio, Hinatuan and Besinga.
With the criminal appeals exhausted at the Ombudsman level, formal Informations will now be filed against the six officials and Bernaldez before the appropriate court.
The investigation was triggered by a complaint filed by Bernard Banal regarding irregularities in Guindulman's 2023 Multi-Purpose Billboard Cell construction project.

According to the Ombudsman's findings, a giant Christmas tree erected in November 2022 was subsequently presented and billed to the municipal government as a newly constructed multi-purpose billboard in May 2023.

Investigators flagged the involvement of the municipal officials in processing, inspecting, and signing off on key transaction records, including the Inspection and Acceptance Report, Certificate of Acceptance and payment certifications, to facilitate the project.
In their appeals, Balo and his co-respondents contended that the project followed legitimate procurement protocols and maintained that they had acted in good faith.
The Ombudsman, however, dismissed their arguments, along with a separate appeal lodged by Bernaldez, ruling that there was no sufficient basis to overturn the initial finding of probable cause.

The anti-graft body maintained that the seven respondents violated Section 3(e) of Republic Act No. 3019, or the Anti-Graft and Corrupt Practices Act, citing evidence of alleged bad faith, manifest partiality, or gross inexcusable negligence.

In denying the motions for reconsideration filed by the respondents in the criminal probe, the Ombudsman stated that it found "no compelling reason to reverse, alter or modify its assailed Consolidated Resolution."
Alongside Balo, the municipal officials facing criminal indictment and dismissal are the following:

items: Rodney Jones Labang, Municipal Engineer
Jean Janiola, Municipal Treasurer
Ariston Beronio, Municipal Engineer
Evelyn Hinatuan, Administrative Aide III
Dennis Theodore Besinga, Administrative Aide II

articles.title: Trump tariff threat ‘unacceptable’, says Brazil, as China denounces levies as baseless
articles.summary: Brazil indignant about proposed tariffs on sugar and aircraft, while Beijing says new levies amount to ‘political manipulation’

blocks.text: Brazil has said it will not bend to the new US tariff “threat” and China accused Washington of “political manipulation” in the wake of Donald Trump’s latest economic salvo against 14 major trading partners.

Brazil’s government said on Wednesday: “Brazil will not yield to this type of threat”, adding in its statement that the “unilateral decision constitutes an unacceptable action within the framework of the ongoing bilateral negotiating process”.
It voiced particular indignation at US proposals for higher import taxes for raw and refined sugar and a new 10% tariff on aircraft, a change that would hit Embraer, Brazil’s largest aircraft maker.

It added that Brazil would continue to negotiate “without ruling out the possibility of adopting retaliatory measures in response to the illegal and unjust imposition of tariffs on Brazilian products”.

Brazil was particularly singled out for in the announcement after trade talks stalled. The Trump administration claimed on Wednesday that the new tariffs would be consistent with trade deals that the US reached last year with dozens of countries.

The new tariffs are being imposed under a law which allowed the president to target countries the US had found to engage in unreasonable or discriminatory trade practices. Jamieson Greer, the US trade representative, told CNBC that many US trading partners had adopted “market distorting practices that tilt the trade balance in their favour while eroding America’s manufacturing base.”
The administration will seek feedback from affected industries and hold a hearing on 25 January, suggesting the final duties won’t take effect until February or March.

China is potentially facing one of the biggest hits. The US said China would face the highest capped rate of 20%, which in some cases will be stacked on top of other import taxes for a total rate of 45%. The US and China last year reached a trade truce but that is set to expire on 10 January 2027.
A spokesperson for China’s embassy in Washington rejected allegations that China was ‌a source of ⁠excess capacity, but stopped short of threatening retaliation.

“The so-called issue of ‘industrial overcapacity’ does not really exist and should not be used as a pretext for political manipulation,” the spokesperson said, urging the two sides to jointly deliver on agreements secured between Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping.

Earlier, China’s foreign ministry restated its opposition while calling for the US to resolve the issue through dialogue. “A tariff war or a trade war serves no party’s interests,” spokesperson Guo Jiakun said.

Greer told CNBC that the administration is proposing a “broad exemption” for $30bn worth of Chinese goods in line with the deal. “We’ve talked to our trading partners about this – they know what we’re proposing,” Greer told CNBC. “I think a lot of this is baked in.”
Some US analysts criticised the duties as too weak to change China’s trade practices.

China “is a bigger source of excess production than the rest of the world combined,” said Derek Scissors, senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute. Yet Wednesday’s proposal “barely raises existing tariffs on China and will make no difference to the country’s trade behaviour.”
Vietnam’s trade ministry said it was ⁠working with the US to complete its trade deal as soon ⁠as possible and would coordinate with relevant US agencies.
It added it was “preparing ​and submitting ​rebuttal comments on the ​preliminary findings as well as on inaccurate submissions ​and allegations ‌made by ​interested ​parties.”

In response to the US announcement, the Indian government denied it had any structural excess capacity in ⁠any sector, ⁠adding that it remained committed to an early conclusion of ⁠a trade deal between the two countries. Greer has said the tariff ⁠on Indian imports would be capped at 17% if a trade deal was struck.
Taiwan was also singled out for new tariffs, but Taipei on Thursday said it was confident it would keep its existing ⁠15% tariff rate.

Taipei and Washington signed trade deals in January and February of ‌this year, which secured preferential treatment for semiconductors and other tech product which account for ​over 70% of Taiwan’s exports to the US.
Other countries and regions affected by the new tariffs include Bangladesh, ‌Cambodia, the European Union, Indonesia, Japan, South Korea, Malaysia, Singapore, Switzerland, and Thailand.
Tokyo’s top government spokesman, Minoru Kihara, said it was “regrettable that a proposed measure targeting Japan has been announced”.

Trump’s latest round of tariffs may be here to stay despite the Democrats’ electoral sweep in the US midterms. Some Democrats will likely support some of the tariffs, particularly on China. And Trump can veto any legislation that seeks to overturn the import taxes.
However Democratic Senator Ron Wyden of Oregon, who will take over the finance committee next year, said he would “use every tool at my disposal to end Trump’s tariffs chaos.”

“This is another blatant attempt by Donald Trump to reconstruct his illegal global tariffs,” Wyden added. “Global overcapacity is a serious problem, but Trump’s unilateral price-hiking tariffs are not the solution.”
With Associated Press and Reuters

articles.title: Crisis aid, medical assistance funds eyed for PhilHealth
articles.summary: Sen. JV Ejercito on Thursday, November 26, explained the rationale behind cutting social welfare allocations to give the Philippine Health Insurance Corp.’s budget a P19.8-billion increase to…

blocks.text: November 26, 2026 | 11:37am
In this undated photo shows people transacting at a Philippine Health Insurance Corp. office.
Philstar.com / Irra Lising

MANILA, Philippines — Sen. JV Ejercito on Thursday, November 26, explained the rationale behind cutting social welfare allocations to give the Philippine Health Insurance Corp.’s budget a P19.8-billion increase to support the implementation of the Universal Health Care Act.
In an interview with DZBB, Ejercito said that his P100-billion target for PhilHealth’s budget may not be reached due to shrinking fiscal space and declining government revenue.
The proposed realignment, however, represents a welcome increase, raising the insurance program’s budget to P94.2 billion from P73 billion.

The funds would come from cuts to the Department of Social Welfare and Development’s Assistance to Individuals in Crisis Situations program and the Medical Assistance Program, with each allocation reduced by P9.9 billion.
According to Ejercito, a larger PhilHealth budget would help expand the insurance program’s coverage and benefits, which can reinforce the Universal Health Care Act.
Under the Universal Health Care Act, every Filipino is automatically enrolled as a member of PhilHealth.
Those able to pay premiums are included as direct contributors. Certain groups, meanwhile, qualify as indirect contributors whose premiums are subsidized by the government.
PhilHealth’s budget funds programs like zero-balance billing, preventive care, immunization and health promotion, as well as enhancements to provincial and local health facilities.

Asked if infrastructure funds could cover the P6 billion needed to meet his budget target, Ejercito said these would remain allocated for their intended purpose, as his priority was to restore funding for foreign-assisted projects.
The allocations for these projects, which include railways and other public infrastructure, saw a P130-billion cut in the House of Representatives’ version of the budget.

This realignment in the House's version, which coincided with an increase in allocations for flood control projects and multi-purpose buildings, prompted intensified scrutiny of the budget at the Senate level.

articles.title: FedEx plane overshoots Miami runway, with flights briefly suspended at airport
articles.summary: The brief ground stop comes on the day before the US Thanksgiving holiday, one of the busiest travel days of the year.

blocks.text: The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has halted flights bound for Miami International Airport in Florida after a FedEx aircraft overran a runway on Wednesday evening.

Departures heading to Miami were grounded just after 20:15 local time (01:15 GMT) and all but one runway at the airport was closed, according to the FAA advisory. Flights are expected to resume by around 22:00 local time, the FAA told the BBC.
The airliner that ran past the runway arrived from Memphis. No injuries have been reported. The FAA is investigating the incident.
The ground stop comes on the day before Thanksgiving, one of the busiest travel days of the year in the US.
Flight delays in Miami reached one hour but appeared to be declining later Wednesday night.
Passengers scheduled to travel on Wednesday night were encouraged to check directly with their airlines for the latest flight updates before heading to the airport.
"We appreciate our passengers' patience as we work to safely resume normal operations," Miami-Dade Aviation Department spokesman Greg Chin said in a statement to the BBC.
The airport is among the top five domestic destinations for travelers in the country over this holiday week, according to the American Automobile Association.
The Miami-Dade area is under a flood watch until late Wednesday night. Periods of heavy rain throughout the day are expected to cause flooding, according to the US National Weather Service.
A nationwide ground stop earlier this month halted flights across the US for hours - the longest such event since the terror attacks on 11 September 2001.

image.caption: The Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade has been pushed back to SaturdayImage: Yuki Iwamura/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: New York's iconic Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade has been postponed for the first time in its 100-year history as extreme weather threatens to disrupt the plans of tens of millions of Americans.
The parade has now been pushed back to 8:30 a.m. EST (1330 GMT) Saturday.
"Our team is now working through the complex operational logistics required to bring the Parade to life on Saturday, and we will share additional details as they are finalized," the company said.
New York City Mayor Zohran Mandani said: "I know that this change of plans will cause inconveniences, yet safety has to come first."
"This will be a heavy storm. We are expecting sustained winds between 30 and 40 miles per hour, with gusts as high as 60 to 65 miles per hour possible," he added.
NBC, which broadcasts the parade, said it will instead show a rerun of the 2025 edition on Thursday.

blocks.caption: NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani said 'safety had to come first'Image: Yuki Iwamura/AP Photo/picture alliance

Despite gale-force winds on the East Coast, coastal flooding in the West and snow in the Midwest, travelers flocked to airports, roads and railways Wednesday for one of America's busiest travel periods of the year.

A major storm developing on the Eastern Seaboard could bring heavy rain, coastal flooding, high winds and power outages to the Carolinas on Wednesday. It is forecast to move to the northern Mid-Atlantic and Northeast on Thanksgiving and is expected to affect air travel at airports in the region.
Already on Wednesday, the security line at New York City's John F. Kennedy International Airport topped one hour.

articles.title: Coalition would privatise Melbourne’s sewage treatment while selling state-owned land and renewables to fund Victorian election promises
articles.summary:
Liberal and Nationals’ pre-election policy costings also reveal that ‘air rights’ between Richmond train station and the MCG would be sold

A Victorian Coalition government would privatise…

blocks.text: A Victorian Coalition government would privatise two sewage plants and sell off state-owned land, renewable energy assets and the “air rights” between Richmond train station and the Melbourne Cricket Ground if elected.
The opposition leader, Jess Wilson, announced a $14.47bn “asset recycling” plan as part of the Liberal and National parties’ pre-election policy costings on Thursday.
She said the plan included a sale of state land to developers, and a $9.2bn, 90-year lease of the Eastern and Western treatment plants that process the vast majority of Melbourne’s sewage.
Wilson said there would be “no change” to water bills as a result of the 90-year lease.
“The reasons why we have made this decision is because we can reduce Victoria’s debt, and what does that deliver? Reduction in interest payments, which cannibalise the state budget,” she said.

The air rights between Richmond station and the MCG would be sold on the condition the station was “revitalised”, while the renewable energy sector would buy the assets owned by the State Electricity Commission, which was only recently revived by the Labor government.
The Coalition has also proposed savings of $5.73bn from drawing down on contingencies and $1.23bn in reprioritising several planned level crossing removals.

The independent Parliamentary Budget Office has found the Coalition’s plan would lower net debt to $176bn by the 2029-30 financial year, compared with $196bn outlined in Treasury’s pre-election budget update this month.
Wilson said it would save the state $4.2bn in interest payments.
More than 1.5 million Victorians have already voted ahead of Saturday’s election.

A U.S. ‌judge on Wednesday barred the Federal Communications Commission from revoking Walt Disney's licences for its eight company-owned ABC TV stations, in a dramatic blow to President Donald Trump's efforts to rein in American media companies.
Ruling is a blow to Trump's efforts to rein in American media firms

"This is not a close case," US District Judge Loren Alikhan wrote. ABC has a "weighty interest in 'vindicating ​their right to be free of retaliation for [their] protected speech,'" the judge wrote ​in a case that was a key test of the free-speech rights of media outlets.
The judge said the FCC appears to be carrying out a retaliatory campaign driven by Trump.
FCC chair ​Brendan Carr, who was tapped to lead the agency in January 2025, "has taken President Trump's ⁠rhetoric as his marching orders," the ⁠judge added.

Trump has repeatedly urged broadcasters to drop ‌comedy or news programs that he dislikes or that have been critical of him or his administration. He has also pressed the FCC on a number of occasions to revoke ABC's licences.
Carr, the White House, Disney and ABC did not immediately respond to requests for comment late on Wednesday.
Reviews ordered in April

Disney and ABC sued ⁠the FCC in August to block an unprecedented early review of licences for eight ABC stations, arguing that the Trump administration was trying to punish the network over its broadcast content.

Carr ordered the reviews in April, even though the stations' licence renewals ‌were not scheduled to be considered before October 2028. The FCC had not ordered an early review in more than 50 years before April.

items: ABC sues U.S. broadcast regulator over early licence reviews, calling it an 'existential threat'
Trump says ABC should fire Jimmy Kimmel over his 'expectant widow' joke

blocks.text: The reviews were ordered in April, a day after Trump urged ABC to fire late-night host Jimmy Kimmel.

Broadcast stations need FCC licences to use public airwaves. While licence revocations ​are extremely rare, critics say the threat of losing a licence can pressure broadcasters and raise concerns about government interference in editorial and programming decisions. Networks have broad ⁠free-speech protections over programming choices.
Jimmy Kimmel’s Melania 'widow' joke | About That

Trump has waged an aggressive series of attacks on the news media and the latest move ⁠follows a two-year-long battle between Trump and Disney. In July, Trump again called for ABC stations to lose their ⁠licences ⁠because the network refused to air a prime-time ​speech on elections.

The FCC is also investigating ABC daytime talk show The View, which discusses U.S. politics, after saying it may ​be subject to federal rules requiring ⁠broadcasters to provide equal-time opportunities to political candidates.
Disney noted earlier that as a result, the program did not invite any political candidates to appear ahead of the November midterm elections, citing the FCC's "pressure campaign."

Trump has also been more broadly criticized by free-speech advocates for attempting to target critics, deport foreign student protesters and freeze federal funds for educational institutions. His efforts have faced legal challenges ⁠and some judicial setbacks.

articles.title: California warned of potential Thanksgiving flooding as storms threaten US coasts
articles.summary: Parts of the Canadian province of British Columbia may also be affected by the storms, which come as millions of people travel for the holiday.

blocks.text: Coastal areas of California are bracing for potential flooding as king tides peak in the state during the US Thanksgiving holiday.

Water levels across the US state's vast coastline could reach over 8ft (2.4 metres) in some areas on Wednesday and Thursday, according to the National Weather Service (NWS) - breaking records set just last month.
The NWS has warned parts of California could face major coastal flooding, which is likely to be significant in low-lying areas. There have already been some reports of flooding.
Meanwhile, storms are also forecast for the Pacific Northwest, including the Canadian province of British Columbia, and eastern parts of the US.
Portions of a pier in northern California came crashing down into the ocean on Wednesday as high tides and strong waves battered the structure, video showed.
Beachgoers have been advised to stay away from the water's edge as large waves could suddenly form. Such waves could be damaging to piers and jetties, and could capsize small vessels, the NWS warned.
Flooding has already been reported in the San Francisco Bay Area.

In San Diego, a high tide of 8 ft 11in was recorded on Wednesday morning local time - potentially breaking the record for highest tide measured in the area, which was just set late last month at 7.98ft.
In Los Angeles, the tide on Wednesday was thought to be as high 8.19 - the record for the city that was set only weeks ago 27 October when parts of the California coast experienced flooding.
Recently set high tide records were also broken in Santa Barbara and La Jolla, according to preliminary data.
King tides are the highest predicted tide of the year and are above the highest water level reached at high tide on an average day.

While they typically occur once or twice a year in most coastal areas, they are happening more frequently in some as sea levels rise. These king tides are being strengthened by the strongest El Niño weather pattern on record.

Storm systems are also expected to impact the US through the Thanksgiving holiday - one affecting the Pacific Northwest and another the eastern part of the country, the US National Weather Service said.
On the east coast, a developing Nor'easter storm is expected to bring heavy rain, strong winds, and coastal flooding.
Major impacts are expected to begin on Wednesday across the southeast, and move northward Wednesday night and on Thursday, the NWS said.
"Those along the eastern seaboard can expect gusty, possibly damaging winds, heavy rain, and major coastal and marine impacts," it added.
The developing storm system could bring about one to four inches rain along America's east coast and a peak of four to six inches in coastal North Carolina.

The US department store chain Macy's has postponed its 100th annual Thanksgiving Day Parade in New York, which was due to take place on Thursday, until Saturday because of severe weather - the first time this has happened.
The stormy weather on both coasts could disrupt travel for millions of people.
The American Automobile Association (AAA) has predicted that 81.5 million Americans will travel at least 50 miles (80km) from home for Thanksgiving between Tuesday 24 November and Monday 30 November.
Officials have also issued a flood warning along Vancouver's coastline in Canada's most western province of British Columbia.
Residents were urged to take "immediate action to protect life and property", a weather warning from Environment and Climate Change Canada said.
King tides were expected to potentially increase already high water levels there too.

articles.title: Poilievre claims constituent's job was threatened after meeting at CFB Wainwright
articles.summary: Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre says one of his constituents — a nurse who helped treat soldiers burned in the CFB Wainwright fire — is having her employment threatened because she met with him.

image.caption: This photo of nurse Maureen Carpenter was posted online by Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre on Oct. 20, 2026. (Pierre Poilievre/Facebook)

blocks.text: Politics·New
Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre says one of his constituents — a nurse who helped treat soldiers burned in the CFB Wainwright fire — is having her employment threatened because she met with him.
Nurse treating soldiers is being harassed, Opposition leader says in House of Commons
In an unusual speech in the House of Commons on Wednesday evening, Poilievre said his parliamentary privilege is being breached.

Last month, Maureen Carpenter was photographed speaking to Poilievre following the fire that killed five soldiers and wounded 38 others on Oct. 17. Poilievre said she is under contract with Calian Health, a government contractor, and works as a nurse.

"Maureen spoke to me on base, with the permission of the unit commander. I had the permission of the base commander to be there. She talked about caring for our men and women on the shift that night, that horrendous night," said Poilievre.

An online post from Oct. 20 shows Poilievre meeting with medical staff at CFB Wainwright Health Services. Online comments identify the woman in the photo as Carpenter, which was confirmed by Poilievre's office.
(Pierre Poilievre/Facebook)

"We owe Maureen as well as colleagues like her, our greatest gratitude. That is what I conveyed in our conversation. Instead, Maureen tells me that she's been threatened by Calian Health, all because she spoke to her local member of Parliament."
Poilievre is the MP for Wainwright, Alta., residents. The base is part of his federal riding of Battle River-Crowfoot.

He said, following the meeting, Carpenter was subject to a complaint and threatened — told by her boss that if her term contract was not already coming to an end, she would be put under the microscope by the company's legal department.
"The implicit message was that her contract would no longer have any chance of renewal, something that she had taken for granted before that point," Poilievre said.
Neither Calian nor Carpenter responded immediately to a request for comment.

Poilievre said Carpenter was told she violated the company's policy by meeting with her MP. He said there is no such policy — there is a rule against speaking to the media, but nothing prohibiting speaking to a member of Parliament.
'My intention was not for this to be politicized': Poilievre raises rare point of privilege

He said being able to speak to an MP is a right guaranteed under the Charter, and a requirement in order to ensure Canadians get good government. During the conversation, he said they discussed better support for mental health following the fires.
He said they did not discuss her company or workplace.
Poilievre said that when he heard from Carpenter, he raised the issue with the minister responsible. His office later confirmed he meant Defence Minister David McGuinty.
McGuinty's office did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
"My intention was not for this to be politicized. I simply wanted it to be solved," Poilievre said.
"Based on his original assurances, I had hoped the minister would put Calian in its place … but her family is indicating that the problems have worsened and there is no end in sight."
Poilievre moved a motion to refer the matter to the procedure and House affairs committee for investigation.

"Ideally though, the government and Calian will instead simply say sorry and fix the problem," he said. "But until and unless that happens, my ability to represent my constituents has been interfered with and you must denounce this conduct."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Kate McKenna is a senior reporter with CBC’s parliamentary bureau in Ottawa, where she covers federal politics. She previously worked for CBC’s The Fifth Estate and in the Halifax, Montreal and Charlottetown newsrooms. Her investigative and breaking news coverage has won five RTDNA awards. She is the author of No Choice: The 30-Year Fight for Abortion on Prince Edward Island.

articles.title: Family of homicide victim Trina Hunt files civil lawsuit against her husband
articles.summary: The lawsuit, filed by Trina's mother, brother and sister-in-law, asks the B.C. Supreme Court to declare that Iain Hunt killed his wife Trina, and make him hand over any property he inherited from her…

image.caption: The remains of Port Moody woman Trina Hunt, 48, were found near Hope, B.C., in March 2021. Now, her family is seeking to have a court declare that her husband Iain killed Trina, and make him hand over any property he inherited. (Twitter/Port Moody Police)

blocks.text: British Columbia·New

The lawsuit, filed by Trina's mother, brother and sister-in-law, asks the B.C. Supreme Court to declare that Iain Hunt killed his wife Trina, and make him hand over any property he inherited from her after her death.
Lawsuit asks court to declare that Iain Hunt killed his wife, make him hand over any property he inherited
A civil lawsuit has been filed against Iain Hunt, the husband of homicide victim Trina Hunt, who was charged with indignity to human remains in relation to her death.

The lawsuit, filed by Trina's mother, brother and sister-in-law, asks the B.C. Supreme Court to declare that Iain killed Trina, and make him hand over any property he inherited from her after her death.
Trina's remains were found near Hope, B.C., in March 2021 — two months after her husband reported her missing from her house in Port Moody.
Police charged him with indignity to human remains in relation to her death, which police have said is a homicide. However, no murder or manslaughter charges have been laid in the case.
Iain Hunt is seen in December 2018. He was charged in February 2025 with one count of indignity to human remains in relation to his wife's death. (Ben Nelms/CBC)
The civil lawsuit states that Iain intentionally misled Trina's family by reporting Trina missing, even though he knew where her body was.

"Mr. Hunt continued the charade by initially participating in a reward for information concerning Trina's disappearance and continuing to assert he knew nothing of her death when he knew all the time that Trina was dead, and he knew the location of her body," the lawsuit states.

items: Attorney general applies to stop disclosure in case against Iain Hunt, citing threat to national security
Court appearance delayed for husband of homicide victim Trina Hunt

blocks.text: The notice of civil claim said that the family relied on Iain's statements as being truthful, which led to concerted public efforts to find the Port Moody woman and raise awareness of her case.
Before Trina Hunt's remains were found, supporters organized extensive search efforts as well as online and in-person campaigns to raise awareness of her case.
Online court records show Iain allegedly interfered with his wife's remains on Jan. 16, 2021, two days before he reported her missing.
Family and supporters of Trina Hunt are seen outside a Port Coquitlam courthouse in March 2025, during an appearance by Iain Hunt. (Ben Nelms/CBC)
'Mental anguish and distress'

The lawsuit says that Iain's actions continue to cause the family "mental anguish and distress," and it seeks special damages for funeral costs and other costs, in addition to making the court hand over any property he inherited.

In the notice of civil claim, Trina's family claims Iain sold the property he co-owned with his wife in May 2023 for $1.92 million, and subsequently bought a property in the rural Fraser Valley community of Harrison Mills.
The family says that property was bought with the funds he obtained by selling the Port Moody house, which he bought with his wife in 2006 for just over $632,000.
Trina's family is seeking a certificate of pending litigation against the Harrison Mills property, as well as a tracing order for all the assets he inherited from Trina after her "wrongful death."

Frank Jang with the Integrated Homicide Investigation Team (IHIT) holds up a picture of Trina Hunt during a May 2021 news conference. Police have said Trina's death is a homicide, but no one has been charged with murder or manslaughter in relation to her death. (Ben Nelms/CBC)

A charge of indignity to human remains "occurs when a person neglects to perform their legal duty to bury a dead human body, or if a person interferes in an improper, indecent or undignified way with a dead human body or human remains," according to police.
None of the lawsuit's allegations have been proven in court.
Iain Hunt's next court appearance, in relation to the indignity to human remains charge, is in September 2027.

articles.title: Brad Pitt, Angelina Jolie settle dispute over French estate Château Miraval

Brad Pitt and Angelina Jolie have reached a settlement in their contentious dispute over the French winery and estate Château Miraval, where they were wed.

"We have settled out of court in the best interests of our family and will not be commenting further," Pitt and Jolie's representatives told CBC News in a joint statement on Wednesday afternoon.
"Any comments in media stories attributed to 'sources' are in fact not coming from either of us, or anyone close to us," they added.

The Château Miraval property in Correns, located in the southern French region of Provence, is seen in 2008. (Lionel Cironneau/Associated Press)

blocks.text: Their split — which involved a bitter custody dispute and allegations of abuse levelled at Pitt — dragged out for eight years, with the A-list Hollywood actors ultimately reaching a divorce settlement in late December 2024.
Duelling lawsuits over estate

In fall 2021, Jolie sold her half of Château Miraval to a wine subsidiary of Russian businessman Yuri Shefler's SPI Group, the international consortium that sells Stoli vodka and other alcohol brands worldwide.
Pitt sued her and Shefler over the sale in 2022, contending that he and Jolie had previously agreed to seek each other's consent before selling their stakes.
Angelina Jolie, second from left, attends the premiere of her movie Maria with her children Pax, left, Zahara, second right, and Maddox in New York in 2024. (Evan Agostini/Invision/Associated Press)

Jolie countersued and — in a subsequent court filing tied to the winery dispute — made public for the first time a raft of details about the in-flight confrontation involving the pair and their children in 2016 that prompted her, days later, to file for divorce.

items: Angelina Jolie describes Brad Pitt's allegedly abusive behaviour in court filing

blocks.text: Jolie alleged in the filing that she and her children had experienced physical and verbal abuse from Pitt while on that private flight, en route from Château Miraval to their home in Los Angeles. The incident was investigated at the time, and no charges were filed against Pitt.
Wednesday's settlement ends the Miraval legal battle between Pitt and Jolie, but Pitt's case against Shefler remains.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

articles.title: Has global jihadism failed, or is it simply changing shape?
articles.summary: Jihadist groups appear to be focusing on local issues rather than global terror. Does it signify a real change?

blocks.text: ByMina al-Lami
Chief jihadist media specialist, BBC Monitoring

blocks.caption: Mina al-Lami

blocks.text: Rice, pasta, sugar, cooking oil and beans are hardly what you'd expect to see in jihadist propaganda. Yet these were among the supplies that al-Qaeda's Somali branch, al-Shabab, said its "charity" had handed out to hundreds of struggling families in August, as it publicised the aid through its social media accounts and radio station.
The group, which controls large parts of rural southern and central Somalia, has been keen to show off its so-called humanitarian work throughout 2026.
"May God reward them," said a local woman in one of al-Shabab's videos.
It's all part of an effort to win over local communities and present itself as more than just a jihadist group.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Al-Shabab has been publicising its humanitarian work

blocks.text: Image source, Telegram
Al-Shabab has been publicising its humanitarian work

A quarter of a century after al-Qaeda's 9/11 attacks in the US, and 12 years after Islamic State group (IS) declared its so-called caliphate in Iraq and Syria, the jihadist movement looks very different.

Rather than focusing on attacking the West or fighting for a global Islamic state, some - especially those linked to al-Qaeda - are putting more effort into winning power closer to home. And they seem increasingly willing to make compromises along the way.

Because of this, a debate is growing within the movement. While hardliners reject compromise, pragmatists see working with local groups and former enemies as a way to gain power. But do the pragmatists represent a genuine change or simply a shift in tactics to achieve the same ultimate goals: establishing a state that applies their strict interpretation of Islamic Sharia law both at home and in its dealings with the outside world?
Significant defeats
Neither al-Qaeda nor IS has achieved its ultimate dream: taking over one or more countries and ruling them according to their strict interpretation of Islam.

Both have suffered major defeats, lost leaders and faced years of international pressure. IS, which once controlled vast areas of Iraq and Syria, lost its last territorial stronghold in 2019. But jihadism hasn't gone away.

Africa is now the main battleground for jihadism, with al-Qaeda's powerful branches, JNIM in the Sahel (Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger) and al-Shabab in Somalia, fighting long-running insurgencies. IS, its bitter rival, has active branches in Nigeria, the Democratic Republic of Congo, the Sahel, Mozambique and Somalia.

One major source of inspiration, and envy, whether jihadists admit it or not, is Syria's new president, Ahmed al-Sharaa. The former IS and then al-Qaeda commander was once wanted by the US but rose to power in Syria in December 2024 and was welcomed by Western leaders.
Once known by his militant nom de guerre Abu Mohammed al-Jolani, he led the jihadist group Nusra Front - initially linked to IS and then al-Qaeda - and later the group Hayat Tahrir al-Sham (HTS).
He gradually broke ties with both IS and al-Qaeda and distanced himself from their calls for global jihad.
Instead, he focused on Syria, building a local power base in the north-western Idlib province.

What surprised everyone was his growing willingness to work with non-Islamist groups and engage with foreign powers. As HTS advanced on Damascus, its leadership sought to reassure the international community, reaching out even to Russia, a key ally of then-president Bashar al-Assad, to allay fears of an Islamist takeover.
That pragmatism, combined with favourable geopolitical conditions - including a weaker Russia and Iran - helped him take power in Syria.
But the sight of him being welcomed by world leaders, including US President Donald Trump, was even more remarkable.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Trump joked with Sharaa when he visited the White House

blocks.text: Image source, AP
Trump joked with Sharaa when he visited the White House
During Sharaa's visit to the White House in November 2025, Trump sprayed him with his own branded cologne, jokingly asked how many wives he had and praised him as a "very strong leader".
For some jihadists, Sharaa's success has been inspiring. Others, however, see his actions as a betrayal of everything they believe in.

IS has declared jihad against Syria's new Islamist government, branding Sharaa and his officials "apostates", and has carried out attacks against government forces on that basis. Other hardline clerics have taken a similar stance, but have stopped short of openly calling for jihad against Sharaa.

The divide between hardline jihadists and their more pragmatic counterparts has fuelled a bitter online debate since 2025, with rival voices trading accusations of betrayal and even publishing competing books to defend their positions.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Sharaa, centre, in 2016, was once a jihadist leader wanted by the FBI

blocks.text: Image source, Reuters
Sharaa, centre, in 2016, was once a jihadist leader wanted by the FBI

For hardliners, going too far can mean abandoning their core beliefs. This might include holding back from imposing their strict version of Islamic law, accepting "man-made" laws or a constitution, taking part in elections, working with non-Islamist groups, or building ties with governments they consider "infidel".

Another source of inspiration for jihadists was the Taliban's return to power in Afghanistan in 2021, as it showed that an Islamist movement could eventually take control of a country after years of fighting Western-backed forces. It engaged local groups, slowly secured power across the country, used international diplomacy, and bided its time before taking the capital, Kabul, in a lightning offensive.
A means to an end?
Two groups are especially worth watching: al-Qaeda's branches in Mali and Somalia.

In late April, al-Qaeda's Sahel branch, known as JNIM, showed considerable pragmatism by joining forces with nationalist Tuareg separatists - whom it had occasionally fought - to launch a major offensive that threatened Mali's military rulers. It even went as far as to call the Tuaregs "brothers".
But it's not just JNIM's growing military strength that's attracting attention. It's also how the group is presenting itself.
Its propaganda once prominently featured al-Qaeda's leaders, slogans and calls for global jihad. Since late 2024, however, its videos have dropped the familiar al-Qaeda branding.
And instead of talking about global Muslim causes, JNIM has increasingly focused on local problems, portraying itself as a defender of ordinary people against corrupt and abusive rulers.
It has repeatedly accused Mali's military government and its Russian allies of killing civilians and making people's lives worse.
In April, it appealed to "all sincere patriots" to help build a "new Mali", promising security, justice and prosperity alongside Islamic law.

It has even suggested it could have "balanced relations" with Russia, despite the fact they're fighting Russian forces backing Mali's government. Its wording echoed that of HTS to Russia as it advanced on Damascus.
There are parallels with Sharaa's approach in Syria: build local alliances, reassure potential enemies and avoid giving outside powers a reason to intervene.
Africa security specialist Aman Bezreh sees similarities between the two groups, but says JNIM's shift may take time.

"JNIM has indeed shown signs of pragmatism similar to HTS", she says. "However, its rebranding has progressed more slowly because the group is simultaneously focused on expanding into new territories and recruiting from diverse pools."
Taliban v Sharaa
The debate over which path to follow is also taking place within JNIM's leadership, according to Wassim Nasr, a France 24 journalist and jihadism expert.

He says one camp favours the Taliban's approach of taking power through force with minimal concessions. The other, which he says currently has the upper hand, favours an approach closer to that of Syria's HTS - making compromises and building wider alliances to gain power more quickly.
Nasr believes JNIM may borrow from both models, but that a break with al-Qaeda is inevitable as a result of its political evolution.
Like JNIM, al-Shabab in Somalia appears willing to make deals with former enemies.

According to Abdullahi Guji, BBC Monitoring's Somalia specialist, al-Shabab reached a truce in October with a powerful Somali tribe, the Ma'awisley, whose fighters had been at the forefront of the fight against the group.
The tribe has since withdrawn its fighters from the front line, dealing a serious blow to the government's campaign against jihadists, says Guji.
Guji believes the group may soon have a chance to test whether it can seize power and establish itself as an alternative government across wider parts of the country.

African Union forces are withdrawing from Somalia amid funding cuts and the approaching end of their mandate in December. Meanwhile, the Somali government is facing political crises and rebellions, creating vulnerabilities al-Shabab could exploit, he adds.
There's another reason some jihadists may see an opportunity to expand: they believe Western governments have bigger fish to fry.
With the war in Ukraine, US-Iran conflict in the Middle East and growing rivalries with China and Russia, fighting jihadists is no longer the priority it was after 9/11.
The US withdrawal from Afghanistan in 2021 and the Taliban's return to power, followed by Sharaa's rise in Syria, have reinforced that belief.

blocks.caption: Image caption, The Taliban has inspired many jihadists

blocks.text: Image source, EPA
The Taliban has inspired many jihadists

Colin Clarke, executive director of the Soufan Center, a non-profit research group that focuses on security, says some jihadist groups have learnt that avoiding confrontation with the US can help them escape Western military action and "live to fight another day".
That doesn't mean the West has stopped fighting terrorism. But if jihadists believe it is distracted or less willing to intervene, they may feel emboldened to pursue power.
History lessons
Unlike its fiercely uncompromising rival IS, al-Qaeda has long shown some flexibility in pursuing its goals. But history offers a warning.

After the 2011 Arab uprisings, which largely sidelined al-Qaeda, affiliated jihadist groups in Yemen, Libya and Tunisia began using the name Ansar al-Sharia (Supporters of Sharia) to win local support without carrying the al-Qaeda brand.

In Mali in 2012, al-Qaeda leaders advised jihadists who had seized the north alongside Tuareg separatists not to rush into imposing strict Islamic rules. Instead, they urged them to work with local allies, avoid alienating communities and play down their al-Qaeda links.
The message wasn't to give up their ambitions. It was to show strategic patience until the time was right. That same thinking could be at work today.

So are these groups really changing their ambitions, or just their tactics? Even those advocating compromise aren't necessarily abandoning their dream of establishing a state ruled by their strict interpretation of Islamic law.
Clarke wonders whether this more pragmatic approach could be a "Trojan horse strategy" – a way for jihadist groups to gain power without giving up their longer-term goals.
"The big question is whether being in power actually moderates these groups, or whether they're simply changing their tactics to survive and strengthen their position," he says.
But not everyone is changing tactics.

IS remains firmly committed to its global ambitions and rejects compromise. Al-Qaeda's Yemen branch, AQAP, continues to call for attacks against the US and Israel, and urges "lone wolf" attacks against Western and Jewish targets.
And it's too early to say whether groups like JNIM and al-Shabab will follow the Taliban or Syrian examples, and whether they're willing to make compromises.
Some jihadist groups may become more focused on local politics as they face the challenges of governing. Others may simply be hiding their wider ambitions until they're strong enough to pursue them.
The global jihadist dream may have failed, but jihadism is far from finished.
Lead image: Reuters/Getty

articles.title: US approves SpaceX plan to send a million data satellites to space
articles.summary: The Starmind constellation aims to be the most cost and energy-efficient way to meet the growing demand for AI computing power.

blocks.text: US regulators have given SpaceX the go-ahead to launch a million satellites into Earth's orbit to help build data centres in space - the first approval of its kind.
The company, which is owned by Elon Musk, wants to use sunlight to power satellites that will process data for AI and send the results back to Earth.
The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) said on Wednesday that the project, known as Starmind, will "support America's booming super intelligence economy".
Its approval comes as communities across the US have pushed back against the expansion of data centres on the ground.

Space X believes the "orbital data centres" are the most cost and energy-efficient way to meet the growing demand for artificial intelligence (AI) computing power that is beyond "terrestrial capabilities".
FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said in a statement that the project "opens a bold new frontier for the computing infrastructure needed to power America's leadership and growth".
"This is the kind of American ingenuity that can unite our strengths in space and advanced technology, reinforce our economic leadership, and expand prosperity here at home," Carr said.
Responding to the announcement, Musk wrote on X: "Much appreciated. This will be a great asset to America and the world."
Under the FCC licence, deployment of the satellites has to begin no later than November 2033. SpaceX will be required to have deployed 10% by November 2035, rising to 50% by November 2038.
The company has already said it wants to launch its first Starmind satellite next year.
Its unclear if a million satellites will be launched or if SpaceX has sought approval for a higher number than it will use.

Like SpaceX's current Starlink network, which provides high-speed internet via more than 10,000 satellites, Starmind's satellites will operate in low-Earth orbit at altitudes ranging between 500-2,000km (310-1,242 miles).
Starmind's satellites will communicate with Starlink's and then relay the data to Earth.

The solar-powered satellite system "promises to bring the human race closer to a Kardashev II civilisation—one that can harness the full power of the sun", the FCC statement said, in a reference to a hypothetical society, proposed by an astronomer in the 1960s, capable of harnessing the entire energy output of its home star.

The orbiting data centre concept is also being explored by other firms - including Google and Blue Origin - and is being pitched as a greener alternative to traditional centres, which require enormous amounts of power to run and water for cooling.
The ever-expanding use of AI computing has seen a massive increase in the amount of data that needs to be stored and processed around the world.

New facilities continue to be built but it is becoming difficult to find places to put them. Data centres are large and sprawling, use enormous amounts of power and water for cooling, and increasingly local people don't want them built nearby.
Data centres were a central issue in the midterm elections earlier in November, with many Democratic candidates promising tougher regulation on their construction.

An expert previously told the BBC that launching hardware into orbit remains expensive and that the infrastructure to protect, cool and power them can be complex - while a growing quantity of space debris puts the physical hardware at risk.
Separately, another cautioned that the growing number of low-orbit craft increases the possibility of crashes between objects - which could damage machines or send materials falling back to earth.
Starlink has been accused of creating congestion in space, something Musk denies. He has also rejected claims his satellites have been taking up too much room and crowding out competitors.
